activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Research on homesickness finds that nearly everyone away from home misses something about it, and roughly 20 percent of university students rate theirs at or above the midpoint of a severity scale.
story:
The elevator in the Ashgrove building smelled like cardboard and someone else's cooking, and Anna rode it to the seventh floor four times before the last box was up. Her mother had decreed that everything must be unpacked by Sunday night, because school started Monday morning and, in her words, they were not going to begin this chapter living out of boxes. Anna had until then to make apartment 7C feel like something other than a place where her shoes were.

The whole move had taken eleven hours of highway. Behind her, two hours west, were the apartment where she had grown up, the corner store that had still sold the old soda brand, and Rachelle, who had cried at the bus stop in a way Anna had not expected from someone usually so pugnacious, someone who argued with referees and once challenged a teacher's grading rubric in front of the whole class. "You'll be back at winter break," Rachelle had said, jabbing a finger at her, as if the leaving were Anna's personal offense. "And you'll text me every day or I'll come get you myself."

There was a smaller memory Anna kept returning to while she slit tape with a house key. Last spring, Zane had stayed over the night before the state finals, and the three of them had lain on her bedroom floor with the lights off, and Zane had said, quietly, that he was terrified of graduating because he didn't know who he was if he wasn't a person who lived on Delmore Street. Anna had laughed at him then. She had said something about how a street couldn't be a personality. She hadn't understood that he was describing a load-bearing wall, and that you only find out which walls are load-bearing when you take one out.

By Saturday afternoon she had assembled her desk, hung the corkboard, and arranged her books in an order that fooled no one, because she kept stopping to look out the window at a parking lot that was not her old parking lot. When her mother suggested she go find the pool on the roof, Anna said yes mainly to escape the boxes. In the stairwell she passed a woman carrying a watering can, who introduced herself as Ms. Sandhu from 7A and said the roof was open until eight, when the landlord locked it.

On the roof there was a girl Anna's age sitting on a lounge chair with a binder open on her knees, highlighters capped and abandoned beside her. The girl looked up, decided something, and said, "You're the new one. 7C. I heard the elevator all day." Her name was not offered immediately; she made Anna earn it, which somehow made it better. She was studying for a placement test on Monday, which was why she was up there instead of in her own apartment, and she said the deadline with the flatness of someone who had stopped pretending it didn't matter.

They talked in the irregular way of strangers who might become friends, and at some point Anna admitted, without planning to, that she had cried in the shower that morning and had then spent an hour pretending to her mother that she hadn't, because being homesick after only one day seemed like a personal failure. The girl, whose name turned out to be Dara, did not laugh. Instead she said, "I looked it up in September when we moved here. Actual research. Nearly everyone away from home misses something about it. Basically everybody." She turned a page in her binder, then added, "And like twenty percent of university students rate their homesickness at or above the midpoint of a severity scale. Twenty percent, at least that." Anna did the arithmetic in her head and found it did not emancipate her from anything, exactly, but it did relocate the problem: it was not a defect in her character but a thing that happened to people, in roughly known quantities, and had been measured by someone with a clipboard and a scale.

Anna tested the idea before she trusted it. "So everyone's a little bit lying about being fine," she said, and Dara said no, most of them probably were fine, just fine and missing something at the same time, which was a different condition. Anna thought of her own mendacity that morning, the cheerful voice she had produced through the bathroom door, and decided she was done practicing it, at least with people who had roofs and placement tests and had also, Dara now admitted, cried in the first week of September, though only once, and only a little.

When the stairwell door clanged open at ten to eight, Ms. Sandhu appeared with her watering can and a small tomato plant she was apparently relocating for the night, and told them the landlord was on his way up with the key. Dara closed her binder and said she'd better go fail to study some more, but at the door she paused and asked whether Anna wanted to see the placement test room on Monday, since she was going that way anyway. Anna said yes before she had finished deciding, and the word was out of her, and there was no taking it back.

That night she texted Rachelle a photo of the roof, the parking lot lights below, the sky going violet over a town she did not yet know, and wrote, "Missed you today, also missed the corner store, also about twenty other things, apparently that's near universal, details later." Rachelle replied within a minute, which meant she had been holding her phone: "EVERY DAY. Starting now." Anna set the phone on the windowsill where she could see it light up, and went back to the last box, the one with her name on it in Rachelle's handwriting, and cut the tape.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: India has marked voters' fingers with indelible ink based on silver nitrate since its 1962 general election, so no one can vote twice.
story:
The registration website asked for her driver's license number, and Addison typed it in with the particular care of someone handling something that might break. Sixteen was old enough to pre-register in her state, the page said; the record would sit dormant until her eighteenth birthday, then wake up on its own. Behind her, her mother dried the same saucepan she had already dried, which was how her mother hovered without admitting to hovering.

On the fridge, held by a magnet shaped like a lemon, was the photograph her grandmother had sent that morning: a close-up of her hand raised like a small flag, forefinger stained violet-black from knuckle to nail. India had finished an election, and every relative in the family group chat had posted the same gesture, the same proud, bruised finger. Addison had screenshotted it and sent it to Savana with a single question mark.

Savana replied while Addison was supposed to be finishing her chemistry homework, which sat open in the next tab, a lab about silver nitrate reacting on a glass substrate, half-written and due Friday. "It's indelible ink," Savana typed. "Silver nitrate. India's been marking voters with it since the 1962 general election, so no one can vote twice." Addison switched tabs and checked it herself, because that was the deal she'd made with herself about the internet: verify, then believe. The election commission's own page confirmed it, the same phrasing, the same year. Her grandmother had stood in a line that started before dawn so that a stranger could paint her finger, and no one in the country could take that mark off and stand in the line again.

"Grandma waited four hours," Addison said to the kitchen. "She sent a whole photo essay."

"Four hours," her mother said, in the tone she reserved for weather and traffic, things that happened to other people in other countries. She set the saucepan down and came to stand behind Addison's chair, close enough that Addison could smell the dish soap on her. "Here it takes ten minutes. If you can find a Tuesday."

Shayna texted then, a small grenade of cynicism: why bother, both candidates were awful, the school board race was between a developer and a man whose entire platform was opposing a bike lane. Addison understood the argument; she'd made it herself in Ms. Popescu's civics class last spring, and Ms. Popescu hadn't rebutted it, had only written a single word on the board, "absolve," and asked whether anyone thought voting was a way of being absolved from other obligations. That had annoyed Addison for a full week before she admitted it was a fair question. Voting once every two years was cheap. Caring was expensive, impecunious in every currency that mattered, and Shayna had decided she couldn't afford it.

But her grandmother had never once, in Addison's memory, described anything as pointless. The same woman who had raised four children on a clerk's salary had stood four hours in the sun for a stained finger, and the mark was silver nitrate, the same compound sitting in Addison's unfinished lab, the same stubborn element that wouldn't wash off. Two ways of seeing it: her mother's arithmetic, ten minutes versus nothing, and her grandmother's testimony, four hours versus nothing. Maybe they were the same position arrived at from opposite ends. Maybe voting wasn't a solution or a sacrament but a way of saying present, the way her grandmother's ink said it, written on skin where nobody could dispute it.

"Fine," her mother said over her shoulder, reading the screen. "Finish it. They'll mail you a card."

Addison hesitated over the party affiliation dropdown, selected the option her grandmother would have argued for, then changed it to no preference, honest about what she hadn't decided yet. She clicked submit, and the confirmation appeared with a reference number she copied into her notes like something valuable.

"Done?" her mother asked.

"Done. In two years I actually vote." Addison turned in the chair. "You'll come with me? For the ten minutes?"

Her mother picked up the lemon magnet, straightened the photograph, and pressed it back against the fridge with more force than the photo required. "I can't, habibti. The green card. You know I'm not..." She let the sentence end where it ended, and began drying the counter that was already dry.

Addison looked at the violet finger on the fridge, then at her own hand on the mouse, clean and unmarked and, in twenty-six months, the only one in this kitchen that would be allowed anywhere near a ballot. She saved her place in the confirmation page, left the chemistry tab open, and stood up to help with the counter.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The 26th Amendment, which set the US voting age at 18, was ratified in 1971 in about three months, faster than any other amendment.
story:
The coffee shop on Delancey had a bulletin board where Ms. Karimi pinned the local election notices, and Oliver had stood in front of it for three weeks pretending to read them while he decided nothing at all. He was seventeen now; he would be eighteen in March, four days before the primary, which meant his birthday gift to himself was going to be his first vote, and he had assumed that wanting to vote was the same as knowing how. It was not. The sample ballot in his pocket had grown soft at the folds from handling, and the two candidates for county executive remained, in his mind, two equally plausible strangers.

He took the window table because it was the only one free, and Denis slid into the opposite chair uninvited, the way he did everything. Denis had opinions the way other people had loose change, always available, always ready to be spent. "Vasquez," he said, tapping the ballot through Oliver's pocket. "It's not complicated. Her opponent wants to cut the library budget to nothing. That's it. That's the whole decision."

"It's not the whole decision," Alivia said, arriving with a cup of tea she had not paid for because Ms. Karimi had a soft spot for students doing homework in her shop, though the shop itself was famously penurious, its chairs mismatched, its espresso machine held together with electrical tape. "The library thing is real, but Brenner actually has a plan for the water system, and the water system is falling apart. You can care about two things."

Oliver said nothing, because the truth was that both of them had already given him their speeches, twice, and the speeches cancelled each other out like weights on opposite pans of a scale. He drank his coffee, which was burnt, and turned his phone over on the table without looking at it.

What he kept returning to instead was Sunday dinner at his grandfather's, two weeks earlier, when he had mentioned offhand that he'd registered. His grandfather had put down his fork. "When I was eighteen," the old man said, "I couldn't vote. None of us could. You had to be twenty-one back then." Oliver had laughed, certain this was one of his grandfather's exaggerations, the same man who claimed to have seen a submarine in Lake Erie. But his grandfather had gone to the shelf and come back with a civics textbook from 1970 and shown him the page, and then, in the voice he saved for things he actually respected, told him about the Twenty-Sixth Amendment, which set the voting age at eighteen, and which was ratified in 1971 in about three months, faster than any other amendment. Oliver had checked it himself that night, half expecting the textbook to be wrong too, and it wasn't. Faster than any other amendment in the whole Constitution. Something that had seemed permanent, the way eighteen-year-olds seemed permanent to him now, had changed in a single spring, before his grandfather was old enough to be drafted but not old enough to vote for the men who ran the draft.

"You're doing the face," Alivia said, waving a hand in front of him. "The one where you're somewhere else entirely."

"I'm thinking about my grandpa. He couldn't vote at eighteen. There was an amendment, nineteen seventy-one, just for that. Three months, start to finish." He hadn't meant to say it like a fact he was proud of, but he noticed that he did say it that way, and then noticed that Denis was already using it.

"See, exactly," Denis said. "People fought to get you that vote, so you owe it to Vasquez."

"That's not what it means," Alivia said. "It means he gets the vote. What he does with it is the part that's his."

The distinction landed on Oliver differently than either of them intended. He had been treating the choice like a debt he owed to someone, his grandfather, the amendment, history, and debts get paid without deliberation. But the vote was not a debt; it was a capacity, the way a hand is a capacity. His grandfather, Oliver remembered, had once told him he'd voted for a man in 1972 he still felt sick about, a small-town autocrat who ran unopposed and cleared the parks of teenagers with a curfew, and his grandfather had voted for him because the alternative on the ballot was worse and because his own father had said so. "The vote I regret," he had told Oliver, "isn't the one I cast wrong. It's the one I cast borrowed." Oliver had not understood him at the time. He was beginning to, and beginning to was as far as it went, because he still did not know whether Brenner's water plan or Vasquez's libraries mattered more to a county he was about to leave for college, whether his vote should be for the place or for the people staying in it, whether eighteen-year-olds who had been franchised by the fastest amendment in the country were supposed to know what they were doing or only to show up and be counted.

He took the sample ballot out of his pocket and smoothed it flat on the table between the two cups, and above the hiss of the espresso machine Ms. Karimi came over with the pot and refilled his coffee without being asked, as though she too were waiting. Alivia leaned in on one side, Denis on the other, and Oliver, with a pencil borrowed from behind the counter, drew a small circle around one of the names, then a smaller question mark beside it, honest about both, and folded it back along its worn creases.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: In the balanced equation 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, two moles of hydrogen gas react with one mole of oxygen gas to form two moles of water.
story:
Vincent had told his father the poster was finished, which was true in the sense that nothing more was going to be added to it. It hung now on the pegboard behind table fourteen, its title lettered in blue marker, STOICHIOMETRY OF HYDROGEN COMBUSTION, and beneath the title a gap where the second graph should have been. He had meant to do the graph. He had, in fact, meant to do all of it properly, and had spent the week instead rereading the one chapter and convincing himself he understood it, which was not the same thing but had felt close enough at midnight.

Eloi arrived first, carrying two coffees and an expression of general grievance. "Heidi's parking the car. She says the lot's full, which I doubt, since it's a Saturday and this is a gymnasium." He set a coffee on Vincent's corner of the table, careful of the balancing point. "Who's the judge?"

"Mr. Yang. From the county office. He does this every year."

"And you know this how?"

"Everyone knows it." Vincent did not actually know it. A girl at registration had said it, and he had absorbed it as fact, the way he absorbed most things, without checking, and now it sat in him feeling solid.

Heidi came in still buttoning her coat, and stood a moment at the doorway looking at the rows of tri-folds and baking-soda volcanoes and one ambitious kid with a tank of fish and a sign about riparian zones and water quality. She came over and read Vincent's poster top to bottom, twice. "Where's the calculation?" she said.

"It's implied by the table."

"Vincent. The whole point is the calculation. Two grams of hydrogen, how much water. That's the project."

"I have the equation." He tapped the board. Two H2 plus O2 yields two H2O. "It's balanced. Both sides match."

Eloi leaned in and counted under his breath, hydrogen atoms on the left, hydrogen atoms on the right, his finger moving above the marker without touching it. "So two moles of hydrogen plus one mole of oxygen gives you two moles of water," he said slowly, as though testing each word on his tongue. "That's the part I actually get."

"That's the part everyone gets," Heidi said. "The part nobody gets is going from grams to moles and back. You take your mass of hydrogen, divide by the molar mass, and then the equation tells you the ratio. Two to two. Then you multiply by eighteen for the water."

"I know that," Vincent said, and heard the falseness in it even as he said it. He knew the sentence. He did not know the doing.

Mr. Yang arrived at the table twenty minutes later, an unhurried man with a clipboard, and asked Vincent to walk him through it. Vincent began with the equation, which was solid ground, and Eloi's count came back to him, two moles of hydrogen gas reacting with one mole of oxygen gas to form two moles of water, and he said it cleanly, and Mr. Yang nodded and waited. Then Vincent reached for the grams and the molar mass and the numbers dissolved. He wrote 2.0 divided by 2.02 and then stopped, pen hovering, because he could not remember whether he multiplied by the ratio before or after, or whether the ratio was one because two over two was one, and if it was one then why did anyone teach it, and the silence in the gymnasium was very specific, the silence of a judge waiting and a friend watching.

"Try the mass you actually measured," Heidi said, from one table over, where she was not supposed to be helping.

"I'm not sure that's permitted," Mr. Yang said, mild.

"I'm not helping. I'm asking about his data." She looked at Vincent. "You weighed the hydrogen in the balloon last night. Four grams."

Four grams. Two moles of hydrogen, then, because the molar mass was 2.02 and four divided by that was about two. And if two moles of hydrogen gave two moles of water, then two moles of water, and two times eighteen was thirty-six. The graph he had never made resolved itself in his head in the space of a breath, grams to moles, moles across the equation, moles back to grams, and he picked up the pen and wrote 36 g and boxed it, and only after boxing it did he look up to see whether it was right, because he could not tell, and that was the honest part, that he still could not tell.

Mr. Yang looked at the boxed number, then at the poster, then at Vincent. "Where's the work between the division and this?"

"At home," Vincent said. "I redid it cleanly."

"In your head just now, you mean." Mr. Yang made a mark on the clipboard that Vincent could not read upside down, and moved on to the fish tanks, and Eloi exhaled beside him like a man released.

"You lied to a judge," Eloi said.

"I told him where it wasn't. That's different." Vincent looked at the boxed number, thirty-six grams of water from a balloon he had weighed at eleven at night in his father's kitchen, and he did not know yet whether the answer held, only that he had built it himself this time, in front of someone, out loud.

Heidi came back and stood at the foot of the table, arms folded. "It's right," she said. "The number. It's right."

"You checked it?"

"Before we parked." She glanced at the gap on the poster where the graph belonged. "So are you going to tell him, or am I?"

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslims who can afford it give a set charity called zakat al-fitr for each family member, so that poor families can also celebrate Eid.
story:
The night before Eid, Lily's mother set an envelope of cash on the kitchen table and began counting it out into smaller envelopes, one for each member of the family, and Lily, who was sixteen and helpful in the way of someone hoping to be trusted with the car keys eventually, offered to finish the job. Her mother was already half out the door to deliver a tray of pastries to the neighbours. She said only, "Remember it's per person, not per family," and then Lily was alone with the money and the arithmetic.

She was sure, in the confident way she was sure of most things that month, that she remembered the rule correctly. The charity before the Eid prayer was a household obligation, one payment covering everyone under one roof, and her mother's instruction had merely confirmed this, since "per person" obviously meant per family in the sense of one household. Lily had a gift for this kind of reasoning, for smoothing contradictions until they stopped bothering her. She divided the cash in half: one envelope for the household of six, one spare.

The next morning the cultural center smelled of cardamom and wet wool, because it had rained on the walk from the car and everyone's coats steamed in the gymnasium heat. Lily found Mariana by the shoe shelves, pulling off damp sneakers, and told her, with some pride, about finishing the envelopes. Mariana's family had arrived from a different city two years ago and knew the customs with a precision that Lily, whose knowledge came partly from overhearing her parents and partly from her own inventions, could only envy.

"You did it per person, right?" Mariana said. "For every single family member."

"One for the whole house," Lily said. "That's how it works."

"It's not." Mariana was not unkind, but she was exact. "It's a set charity for each family member, so the poor families can celebrate Eid too. My dad does five envelopes. Five kids, five envelopes."

Lily's certainty did not collapse all at once; it retreated and defended itself. She thought of arguing, of citing her mother, and then she remembered her mother's actual words on the way out the door and felt the ground shift under her. She had heard what she expected to hear. She had a habit of dichotomizing the world into things she knew and things that didn't matter, and this had clearly fallen, wrongly, into the second pile. It was a pernicious little habit, comfortable and quiet, the kind that never announces itself as a flaw until it costs you something, and this morning it had cost her five envelopes.

The prayer line was forming at the far end of the gymnasium. Mr. Hussain, who taught Sunday classes and organized the center's collections, stood by a folding table with a cash box, and Lily understood that the money was meant to reach him before the prayer began, not after. There was no time to go home. Her stomach performed one tight turn, and then, instead of the panic she might have allowed herself, she found a strange reprieve in the clarity of the problem: it was only money, and she knew where to get it.

She found her father near the water fountains, explained in a low voice that she had gotten it wrong, that it was meant to be a set amount for each of them, six times over, and that she had counted it as one. He did not lecture her. He counted out the difference from his wallet, unhurried, and said, "Your mother told you per person." It was not a question. Lily said yes, she had, and she had heard it as something else, and she was sorry. Her father put the bills in her hand and said, "Then go fix it before the imam starts."

At the folding table she gave Mr. Hussain the corrected amount and, because honesty seemed the only durable option, told him exactly how she had miscounted. He laughed, a short warm sound, and said half the families at the center had made that mistake at least once, including him, decades ago in a mosque in another country. He dropped the bills into the cash box and wrote her family's name on his list, six marks beside it, one for each of them.

Walking back toward the prayer rows, Lily turned the morning over without trying to resolve it entirely. She had been wrong, then she had been right enough to fix it, and somewhere between those two states was a way of holding her own knowledge more loosely, though she could not yet say how that would feel the next time she was certain of something. Mariana caught her eye from the third row and raised an eyebrow. Lily held up six fingers and grinned. The imam stepped to the front, and the whole gymnasium went quiet at once, coats still steaming.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Cheating out means an actor turns their body partly toward the audience, even while talking to another character, so their face and voice carry.
story:
The gym smelled of varnish and cold rubber, and the stage they had built from risers sat under the basketball hoop like something that had been extruded from the school itself, plain and temporary. Layla stood at the edge of it with her binder open to the pages she had covered in arrows. In three weeks the drama class would perform her one-act in front of the whole tenth and eleventh grade, and tonight, in the empty gym with the overhead lights making everything flat, she was going to figure out why the play kept looking wrong.

She had wanted this since November, since she had watched the senior director stand exactly where she was standing now and say "hold" and have everyone actually stop. Layla had applied with a script she had found in the library's basement shelves, a small argument between two sisters over a stolen letter, and Ms. Rosen had handed it back with a single word on the cover: yours. That word had felt like a door. Now it felt more like a weight she kept setting down and picking up again.

Haiden played the older sister. Larissa played the younger. They ran the second scene, the one Layla had rewritten twice, and Layla sat on the floor in the third row of folded bleachers the way an audience would, chin on her knees. The dialogue was fine. The pauses were fine. But when Haiden turned to Larissa to deliver the accusation, all Layla could see was the back of her head, a dark curtain of hair, the words arriving at the bleachers muffled and secondhand.

"Hold," Layla said, and both of them stopped, and something in her chest kicked, because they had stopped. She walked down onto the risers. "Haiden, when you talk to her, you're facing her all the way. I can't see your face. I can barely hear you."

"That's where she is," Haiden said, reasonably. "I'm talking to her, not to the bleachers."

"I know. But it's like the whole fight is happening in a room I'm not in." Layla turned her own body to face Larissa the way Haiden had, said a line at her, heard her own voice die somewhere near the foul line. Then she angled herself, kept her eyes on Larissa, opened her shoulders halfway toward the empty bleachers, and said it again. The line carried. Her face was visible and still honest, still aimed at her scene partner. She stood there a second, surprised.

"Larissa," Layla said, "did you ever hear if there's a name for this?"

"There is," Larissa said. "My cousin does community theatre. It's called cheating out. You turn your body partly toward the audience, even while you're talking to another character, so your face and voice carry."

Haiden tried it once and overdid it, facing the bleachers so squarely it looked like she was addressing a jury. The second try was better: three-quarters to Larissa, one-quarter to the house, her chin still lifted toward her sister. Layla watched the scene from the bleachers again and this time she could see the moment the accusation landed, the small flinch Larissa let cross her face before she answered. It was like watching a different play. She marked the arrows in her binder differently now, not straight lines but soft diagonals, every confrontation pulled a few degrees toward the dark.

She remembered, while they reset, a choice she had made in auditions that she still hadn't settled in herself. She had cast Haiden over a girl who had acted longer and wanted the role more visibly, wanted it with a hunger Layla had found faintly uncomfortable to sit across from. Layla had told herself she chose Haiden because the stillness fit the sister, which was partly true and partly a veneer over the other truth, that she had been afraid of the wanting girl and comfortable with Haiden, who was easy and funny and a friend. Directing kept handing her these small verdicts about people, and she kept signing them without being certain she had read the evidence.

They ran the scene six more times. On the fourth, Haiden cheated out without being reminded and Larissa matched her, and the rhythm between them tightened into something Layla had not written, something that had only become available once their bodies agreed to include the audience in the room. Layla caught herself thinking about ancillary things that suddenly weren't ancillary at all: the angle of a chair, where a pause breathed, whether an audience could forgive a character they could see clearly. The script was only part of it. Maybe the smaller part.

"Once more, then water," Layla said, climbing back up to the bleachers. Somewhere above them a door banged and the janitor's cart squeaked down the hallway outside, indifferent. Haiden and Larissa took their places on the bare risers, under the hoop, in the flat light.

"From the top of the scene," Layla called, and raised her hand, and brought it down.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier.
story:
Xavier set the dense little loaf on the counter of the community kitchen and waited for someone to say it was fine. Nobody did. Hans poked the crust with one finger, and Zachary turned it over like a suspect object, and Mr. Mercer, who ran the Thursday night cooking group, only raised his eyebrows and handed Xavier a bread knife.

His mother had started the double shift at the hospital that morning, and his father was still in the casts from the scaffolding fall, so the meal had fallen to Xavier: soup from the church pantry box, and bread, because his mother had said bread makes it a meal instead of soup. The soup was fine. The bread had come out like a brick with a hat of crust, and when he cut it, the inside crumbled into gravel.

"I kneaded it," Xavier said. "I did what it said." He'd folded and pressed for maybe four minutes, watching the clock because his younger sister needed picking up, because the laundry needed moving, because there was always something.

Mr. Mercer slid a second bag of flour across the counter. "Try again," he said. "You've got an hour."

Zachary leaned against the sink, arms crossed, in the way of someone with advice he was saving. "My aunt says bread either works or it doesn't," he offered. "It's the flour. Some batches are just bad."

"You think the flour did it," Xavier said.

"I think flour's flour. You didn't do anything wrong." Zachary said this kindly, the way you tell someone it wasn't their fault, but it had the flatness of a platitude, a thing said to close the subject rather than open it, and Xavier found he didn't want to be comforted. He wanted the loaf to be better.

He measured again, and this time, while the yeast foamed, he cleaned out his phone's cracked screen with his sleeve and looked it up. Hans drifted over, ostensibly to check the oven timer, actually to read over his shoulder. The screen said that gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water. "So it's not the flour going bad," Xavier said slowly. "It's proteins making something new once the water's in." And kneading longer, the screen went on, makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier. He read that line twice.

"Then your first one," Hans said, tapping the dead loaf, "you barely worked it. Four minutes, you said."

"So it's my fault." It came out strange, almost relieved. If the kneading was the problem, then the kneading could be fixed, and in a way that exonerated the flour, the recipe, the whole indifferent machinery of bread. He wasn't being defeated by bread. He'd just stopped early.

He kneaded the second dough and kept going past the point where his shoulders complained, ten minutes, then more, and the dough changed under his hands, stopped tearing when he stretched it, went smooth and strange, like something that had decided to hold itself together. Zachary wandered back and watched. "My aunt also says don't fight the dough," he said.

"I'm not fighting it. I'm building it." Xavier stretched a piece thin enough that light came through. "Gluten. That's what this is."

Zachary was quiet for a moment, which for him was a long time. "So when my aunt's loaf comes out like yours did," he said, "it might not be the flour."

"Might not be."

"That's going to be a hard conversation."

They both laughed, and Mr. Mercer, wiping down the far counter, didn't look over, but the corner of his mouth moved.

While the loaf rose, Xavier portioned the soup and thought about which was truer, what he'd believed an hour ago or what he believed now, and had to admit he didn't fully know. Maybe some loaves did fail for no reason, flour or weather or bad luck, and his hands had only been one cause among several. He had one good loaf's worth of evidence and a pithy line from a website, and a person could build too much certainty on too little kneading, in bread or anywhere else. He decided he'd hold the new idea lightly, the way he now held the dough.

When the loaf came out, tall and browned and hollow-sounding when he knocked its base, Hans cut a slice while it was still too hot, against all advice, and butter ran into the crumb, which tore soft and chewy instead of crumbling. Xavier wrapped the second half in a clean towel for his father, who would be awake at midnight wanting something to eat with his tea.

"Take some for your sister," Mr. Mercer said, sliding a small wrapped piece toward him, already cut.

Xavier put it in his bag with the soup container, and on his way out the door he turned back to the counter where the first loaf still sat, halved and gray-hearted, and picked up a piece of it too.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: The doctrine of double effect, traced to Thomas Aquinas, holds that causing a harm one foresees but does not intend can be permissible when it is a side effect of pursuing a good end.
story:
Mr. Traoré had written one sentence on the board before the bell finished ringing: "Can a good action excuse a bad result?" Maika copied it into her margin, then stopped, because she already knew the answer, or thought she did, and the knowing sat badly in her stomach.

Two seats over, Mckenna was already talking. "Obviously if you help someone and someone else gets hurt, you're still helping. That's just math." Nikola leaned back with the particular patience of someone preparing to disagree. "It's not math, it's who counts. The person you hurt counts exactly as much."

Maika said nothing. She was remembering the fourth floor of St. Brendan's, where she volunteered on Thursday evenings, restocking the family lounge with crackers and bad coffee. She had been carrying a tray past an open door when she heard the doctor, an older woman with reading glasses pushed up into her hair, speaking to a resident in a low, flat voice. "We increase the pain relief. We can see it may shorten her time. But the intention is her comfort, not the ending of her. That distinction matters. Aquinas called it the doctrine of double effect." The resident nodded. Maika stood in the hallway with her tray of crackers until a nurse asked her if she was lost.

"Maika," Mr. Traoré said. "You've gone somewhere. Want to bring it back?"

She hadn't planned to speak, but the memory was already out of its drawer. She told them about the hallway, the doctor's words, the phrase she had written on her phone that night so she wouldn't lose it. "Something about a harm you foresee but don't intend," she said. "That it can be permissible when it's a side effect of pursuing a good end. I looked up Aquinas later. It's an old idea. Medieval old."

Nikola turned fully toward her. "So the doctor was excusing herself."

"I don't think so," Maika said, and heard how uncertain it came out, so she pushed on. "She sounded like someone who had decided and still wasn't comfortable. Like the distinction let her act, not feel fine about it."

Mr. Traoré raised a hand, not to answer but to slow them down. "Notice what Maika just did. She's holding two descriptions of one act. Which is truer?"

"Both," Maika said, before she meant to.

After class, Mckenna caught her at the door. "That was visceral, the way you told it. I actually felt the hallway." Mckenna was always generous like that, handing out compliments the way other people handed out gum. "But you should write to that doctor. Ask her how she lives with it."

"I can't," Maika said. "Volunteers don't email doctors."

"So write and don't send it. That's a thing people do."

That night Maika did write it, at her desk with her philosophy binder still open, and she did not send it. "Dear Dr. whoever you were, fourth floor, Thursday evenings. You probably don't remember me. I was the girl with the crackers. I want you to know I've been trying to cogitate on what you said, not just react to it, and it's harder than I expected. My teacher put a question on the board and I thought of your voice in the hallway. Here is what I keep circling: if intention is what separates the permissible from the wrong, then the person who is harmed by the side effect has to trust the story the agent tells about herself. The woman in the bed can't audit anyone's intention. She just gets the shorter time. Maybe the doctrine is true and also not enough. I'm eighteen, so probably I'm wrong in some way I can't see yet. Anyway. I hope her comfort was real. I hope someone held her hand."

She read it twice, then folded it into the back of her binder, behind the notes on Mr. Traoré's sentence, which she had annotated in the margin: "foreseen / intended / side effect / good end." Four phrases, and underneath them she had started to write "but the harm is still real to the person it happens to," and crossed out "still," because the word added nothing, and because crossing it out felt like a small act of honesty.

The next Thursday she was back on the fourth floor, restocking the lounge. The hallway door was open again, the same room, a different bed. She stood where she had stood before. Down the corridor a television murmured, and somewhere a machine kept its patient rhythm, and the crackers in her hands smelled like nothing.

A nurse came out of the room and saw her. "You can go in, if you like," the nurse said. "She likes company."

Maika looked down at the tray, then at the doorway, and stepped forward.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Under US federal child labor rules, workers under 18 may not operate power-driven meat slicers, even in a grocery store deli or restaurant.
story:
The hardware store smelled of cut pine and machine oil, and David stood at the register in a green apron that was still stiff at the creases. He had been hired two days earlier, on a Tuesday, after an interview in which the manager asked him only three questions and then said the job was his if he could work Saturdays. He could work Saturdays. He needed the money for something he had not yet named aloud, even to himself, though his mother had started saying "college" in the tone people reserve for weather they cannot change.

On his third shift the manager came through the aisles at a pace that made the paint stirrers rattle in their bin. "Delgado didn't show at the deli next door," he said. "Ms. Sandhu's short-handed, lunch rush coming. I told her I'd send someone. You. It's just the slicer and the scale, ten pounds of turkey, how hard can it be."

David did not move right away. Through the front window he could see the deli's neon sign, the color of a strawberry candy, and behind its glass a machine with a circular blade turning idly, catching the light. Something in his chest went quiet, the way a room goes quiet when a door has been left open somewhere in the house.

"I can do the scale," he said. "Register, tomatoes, whatever. Not the slicer."

The manager's eyebrows came together. "It's a slicer, not a lathe. Delgado runs it and he's got the brains of a mop."

"I'm seventeen." David kept his voice level, the way he had practiced in the car on the way here, though he had not known he would need the practice so soon. "Federal child labor rules. Workers under eighteen can't operate power-driven meat slicers. Not even in a grocery store deli or a restaurant." He had read it that morning, actually read it, on the labor law poster sequestered behind the time cards in the break room, in the corner where nobody looked, the fine print he'd always skimmed the way everyone skims it. He had read it twice and then a third time with his thumb on the line, because of a thing he did not talk about.

The manager stared at him. Outside, a woman in a hairnet was waving from the deli's doorway, a wave that meant hurry. "You're telling me a law stops you."

"The law stops both of us," David said. "It's just that I'm the one it names."

The manager went to the phone, and David was left for a moment in the fluorescent hush of aisle five, between the duct tape and the sandpaper, feeling the strange liminality of being seventeen, old enough to be trusted with a register and a set of keys to the stockroom, young enough that the government had drawn a line around certain machines and written his age on the near side of it. Harmony appeared from the plumbing section with a box of washers balanced on her hip. She had trained him on the register on his first day, and she had a way of watching things without turning her head.

"He could've asked me," she said. "I covered the deli in June, before my birthday." She set the washers down. "You know how I found out about the rule? Somebody from the state came in. Ms. Sandhu got a warning letter. Not a fine, just a letter, but she framed it, hung it by the cold cuts like a diploma."

David looked at her. "She framed it?"

"She says it saved her from a worse thing." Harmony shrugged, adjusting the box. "She doesn't say what the worse thing would have been."

The manager came back. His face had rearranged itself into something David couldn't read, part irritation and part something older and more careful. "Delgado walked in, sick as a dog but vertical. Ms. Sandhu says you're off the hook." He looked at David for a long second. "Where'd you learn that, anyway? The rule."

"The break room poster," David said.

"You read those?"

David buttoned the top of his apron, which had come loose, and thought about how to answer, and decided on part of it. "My brother worked at a sandwich place when he was my age," he said. "Different machine, a dough mixer, that one's legal at seventeen with training. He still has all his fingers, but the guy on the next station didn't keep all of his. So yeah. I read those."

The manager absorbed this without comment, then went back toward the office, pausing at the corner of the aisle. "Saturdays still work?" he said, and it was not really a question, or it was a different question than the words themselves.

"They work," David said.

He didn't feel the seismic thing he had expected, no floor shifting under him, just the ordinary hum of the refrigerator case and the smell of pine. He rang up a woman buying a hacksaw, counted her change into her palm, and through the window watched the slicer in the deli next door spinning its bright circle, turning now under Delgado's gray hands, legal hands, older hands, a machine that would never know his name.

At the end of his shift Ms. Sandhu herself came into the hardware store, still in her hairnet, carrying a wrapped sandwich. She set it on the counter in front of David without ceremony.

"Turkey," she said. "Sliced by a man of lawful age. You want the job on Sundays too, it's yours, register and tomatoes only." She tapped the sandwich once with two fingers. "Eat it while it's fresh, David."

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Schenck v. United States (1919), Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic.
story:
Tyler had drawn both sides of the same case, which meant that by Friday afternoon he would have to argue against himself in front of a panel of real judges in the chamber at city hall. The notice had gone up on Monday: each student in Mr. Leung's constitutional law elective would be assigned a landmark First Amendment case, and Tyler, because he had been last to the sign-up sheet, got the leftovers. Schenck v. United States, arguing for the government in the morning round and for the petitioner in the afternoon.

"It's actually a gift," Terrance said on the walk downtown, carrying the cardboard box of briefs like it was a pizza he'd paid for himself. Terrance had gotten one side only, Tinker, and he wanted the trophy badly, the small brass gavel that the bar association gave the top advocate, because his mother had promised to drive in from the coast to watch the final round. "You get to know the case twice as deep as anyone."

"Or I get to lose twice." Tyler held the door of city hall for a woman balancing a tray of coffee, and she nodded thanks, and Terrance's elbow nudged him forward because they were late for check-in.

The chamber smelled like floor wax and old paper. Mr. Leung was setting out name placards at the counsel tables and did not look up when they came in. "Five minutes to rounds," he said. "Mr. Reyes, you're first, government side, Department of Justice table." He said it the way he said everything, flat, but he had left a bottle of water and a stack of sticky notes at each seat, and Tyler noticed that his had a second stack, extra, as if someone had counted the arguments he'd have to make.

The morning round went badly, then well, then badly again. A judge with reading glasses pushed up into her gray hair asked why distributing leaflets opposing the draft should be unprotected speech, and Tyler gave the standard answer about wartime, about clear and present danger, and felt the words slide off her like water off an impermeable coat. It was in the rebuttal that he reached for the famous line. "Free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic," he said. "Justice Holmes wrote that in the opinion itself, in 1919." The judges nodded. He sat down having won the round, and having hated winning it.

Because in the hallway, during the break, he had opened the packet Mr. Leung had left in the box, the photocopies with the margins already annotated, and there it was in the opposing counsel's practice notes: the same line, flagged, with a question mark beside it in pencil. Tyler read the question twice. Who wrote that line, and when, and against whom? Holmes. 1919. The same man who upheld the conviction of the pamphleteer, in the same opinion, in the same breath. The government's most quotable defense of punishing speech was written by the very judge doing the punishing.

He found Terrance by the water fountain, rehearsing under his breath, hands moving through the shapes of his argument. "I have to argue the other side in ninety minutes," Tyler said, "using the quote I used this morning to sink the other side."

Terrance stopped mid-sentence. He looked at Tyler, then at the clock over the stairwell, and Tyler could see him doing the arithmetic of his own prep time against a friend's emergency. "Ten minutes," Terrance said. "I'll give you ten minutes of my lunch block. Cross-examine me. Be the judge, be terrible to me, I don't care, just say the line at me so you have to answer it."

They sat on the marble steps by the restrooms and Terrance, chewing half a sandwich, played the panel. "Counsel, if the great Justice Holmes himself said free speech would not protect a man falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic, on what basis do you ask us to overturn him?"

Tyler tried three answers aloud and discarded each one. The first was evasion. The second was flattery, and Terrance called it that, mouth full. The third one Tyler made himself say slowly: "The same pen that protected the theatre also sent Charles Schenck to prison for leaflets. The question isn't whether Holmes was quotable. The question is whether the theatre and the leaflets belong in the same sentence."

"You're allowed to say that?" Terrance said.

"I don't know," Tyler said. "That's the part I can't look up."

When the afternoon round began, the chamber had filled; Terrance's mother had arrived early, coat still on, and sat in the second row, and Mr. Leung had to ask her, gently, twice, to turn off her phone camera flash. Tyler stood at the petitioner's table, the wrong table from the morning, the light coming through the tall windows at a different angle across the same floor. The judge with the reading glasses raised her hand almost at once.

"Counsel," she said, "your adversary this morning quoted Justice Holmes to you. Falsely shouting fire in a theatre. How do you answer that?"

Tyler let one breath go out. "I'd ask the court to historicize the line before it's used against my client. In 1919, Holmes wrote it while upholding a conviction for anti-draft leaflets. The sentence everyone remembers and the sentence nobody quotes came from the same opinion. If I stand here and pretend the theatre proves the leaflet, I'm not making an argument, I'm borrowing a costume." He paused, aware of the panel's stillness, aware he was further out on the ice than any brief had authorized. "Maybe the theatre really is different from the leaflet. I haven't resolved that, and I'd distrust anyone my age who claimed they had. But the burden of showing they're the same belongs to the government, and the government has offered only the echo of a famous man."

The gray-haired judge took off her glasses and wrote something long. Mr. Leung, at the side table, made no mark in his grading sheet at all, which was the most unnerving thing Tyler had seen all day, though when Tyler sat down he found that the second stack of sticky notes had been moved next to his water bottle, and on the top one, in Mr. Leung's cramped hand, a single word: "again."

Terrance's final round was called before the scores were posted. He stood, straightened his tie, and pressed the gavel-shaped trophy pamphlet flat under his binder, and his mother leaned forward in the second row with her hands folded like a prayer. Tyler took out a pen and wrote at the top of a fresh page: "Question for Holmes: who was in the theatre?"

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Marx and Engels's Communist Manifesto of 1848 opens its first section by claiming that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.
story:
The book club met on Tuesdays in the library's back room, where the radiators clanked and someone had taped a lugubrious poster of a crying owl above the recycling bin, as though even the waste knew something about despair. Savannah arrived early with her copy of Jane Eyre and a photocopy from Ms. Ferreira's critical theory binder, folded twice in her back pocket. She had a presentation Thursday. She needed it to be more than the paragraph she'd written at midnight, the one that said Mr. Rochester was "problematic" three times and then trailed off into ellipsis.

"Is that a highlighter or a weapon?" Alayna asked, dropping into the chair beside her.

"It's four highlighters. I'm building a taxonomy." Savannah spread them out: green for things Charlotte Brontë seemed to know she was doing, orange for things she didn't, blue for things the critics said, and yellow, which Savannah hadn't used yet because yellow was reserved for whatever she actually figured out on her own.

Aimee came in last, carrying the wrong book entirely. "Okay, so, my grandfather lent me this because he heard we were doing critical lenses and he has opinions." She held up a small pamphlet, its cover gone the color of weak tea. "He says you can't understand any novel without this."

Ms. Ferreira, shelving returns at the back, raised an eyebrow but said nothing. She had a policy about letting them arrive at their own catastrophes.

Aimee flipped to the first page and read aloud, doing a gruff voice she clearly intended as an impression of her grandfather: "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. That's how it starts. First section, dead-on. Written in 1848." She lowered the pamphlet. "So does Jane fit? Is that the book? Rich guy, poor governess, big house burns down?"

"That's Marxism," Savannah said, and then heard how dumb that sounded, since Aimee obviously knew that, since her grandfather had an entire shelf about it. "I mean, that's the lens I'm supposed to be presenting. Along with feminism. I have to do both."

"So do both at once," Alayna said, chewing the cap of her pen.

"It doesn't work at once. That's the whole problem." Savannah pulled out the photocopy and found the passage she'd flagged, the one where Jane tells Rochester she is not a bird caught in a snare, that she is a free human being with an independent will. "Look. Feminist me reads this and wants to stand on a chair. This is 1847 and she's saying it to her employer. But then Marxist me remembers that her independent will is employed at thirty pounds a year, and the wedding that gets interrupted exists so that a man of property can regularize his claim on a woman he'd otherwise keep in a third-floor attic like an old trunk."

"Stand on the chair anyway," Alayna said. "Both things can be true."

"Both things can be true, but they can't both be the whole thing." Savannah tapped the pamphlet where Aimee had left it open. "If all history is class struggles, then Jane's will is shaped by money whether she knows it or not. But if I only read it that way, then her saying no stops being brave and starts being, I don't know, inevitable. Like she was going to say it because history scheduled her to."

Aimee squinted. "My grandfather would say you're abrogating individual agency, and then he'd make you tea."

"He'd be right about the word, anyway." Savannah uncapped the yellow highlighter, then didn't use it. "Here's what I can't get past. The class thing explains why she's poor and why the marriage would fix it. It does not explain why she walks away from the marriage. Nobody made her do that. Charlotte Brontë made her do that."

Ms. Ferreira drifted over and slid the last book onto the shelf. "You know you're allowed to end a presentation with a question," she said. "It's even encouraged, at your age. Later they'll want answers, and you can decide then whether to give them." She pointed at the crying owl poster on her way back to the desk. "Also, whoever made that owl should be found and stopped."

Savannah wrote in the margin of her photocopy: the history of class struggles is the frame, not the picture. Then, beneath it, in smaller handwriting: is that enough? She left the yellow highlighter lying flat on the table, unopened, a color still waiting for a claim it could prove.

Alayna leaned over and read the margin. "Thursday, when they ask, what do you actually say?"

Savavenport looked at Jane Eyre, then at the pamphlet with its tea-colored cover, and capped the green highlighter. "I say Jane's free will is real, and it's also the one thing the class analysis can't buy." She gathered the books into her bag. "And then I ask the class to fight me about it."

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Sabbath commandment appears twice in the Hebrew Bible with different reasons: Exodus 20 cites God resting after creation, while Deuteronomy 5 cites Israel's release from slavery in Egypt.
story:
Ryder spread the two photocopies across the kitchen table, one beside the other, the way Mr. González had shown him after class: not stacked, but side by side, so his eyes had to travel. The plan was simple, or had seemed simple in the empty classroom. For Monday's debate he had to argue whether the Sabbath commandment still applied in modern life, and Mr. González had imposed one strange rule, that every claim had to come from the text itself, no Wikipedia, no sermon podcasts, no appeals to what everybody already knew. "The text," Mr. González had said, "is the only witness you're allowed to cross-examine."

The problem revealed itself slowly, the way a photograph develops. Ryder had assumed the commandment appeared once and that would be that, but there it was in Exodus 20, in the middle of the Ten Commandments, and there it was again, nearly word for word, in Deuteronomy 5. Nearly. He leaned over the pages with his cold toast forgotten at his elbow and ran his finger down the lines. Remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy. Same opening. Then the reasons forked like a road splitting outside a town. Exodus said God made the heavens and the earth and rested on the seventh day. Deuteronomy said something else entirely, something about Egypt, about being a slave there and being brought out by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm, therefore keep the day. He read both endings three times. Why would one law need two different reasons?

The kettle ticked as it cooled. His mother came through in her work uniform, glanced at the papers, and said he looked like a lawyer preparing for trial, which he took as a compliment until he realized lawyers were supposed to know their argument by now. His counterargument was due to Marko by tonight. They had divided the work over lunch: Ryder took the text, Marko took the modern-life side, and together they would rehearse against each other until neither could be surprised. But the text had ambushed him before Marko even arrived. If the commandment gave two reasons, then the whole question of what the rule was for had two answers, and answers, in his limited experience of arguments, were the parts people fought over most.

Miya arrived first, letting herself in through the back door the way she always did, shaking rain off her jacket. She was on the opposing team, which everyone had decided was fine because it wasn't personal, and she dropped into the chair across from him and pulled the Exodus page toward her without asking. "This is the one my grandmother has framed," she said. "Creation. God rested, so we rest." She said it with the settled certainty of someone quoting the family china.

"Read this one," Ryder said, sliding Deuteronomy across the table.

She read. Her lips moved slightly, which he pretended not to notice. "Slavery," she said finally. "It's the same commandment and the reason is slavery?" She looked up. "Why does nobody mention this?"

"That's what I keep asking." He tapped both pages. "One book says rest because God rested after making everything. The other says remember that you were slaves in Egypt and you were brought out, so give your workers the day too. It's the same rule with a completely different engine underneath it."

Miya sat back. "So which one is the real reason?"

"I don't know if that's the right question." He heard himself say it and was surprised, because an hour ago the right question had seemed like the only thing he was looking for. "Maybe the rule can hold both."

Marko came in at six with his backpack and a bag of chips, already doctrinaire, already armed with the case he'd built: modern life, hospital shifts, gig economies, the impossibility of a whole society stopping on the same day. He delivered it at the counter while pouring himself water, fluid and merciless. The commandment was beautiful, he conceded, and obsolete, a relic from an agricultural world that had every right to its rest and none to ours.

"Which commandment, though?" Ryder asked.

Marko frowned. "The commandment. There's one."

"There are two versions." Ryder laid the pages side by side again and made Marko read both, watched his eyes move down the column the way Miya's had. When he finished, Marko read it a second time, and the kitchen was quiet except for the refrigerator's hum.

"Okay," Marko said slowly, "but which one do we argue against?" He had expected to fight a rule about imitating God, something cosmic and easy to call outdated. The second version was harder to dismiss. Nobody thought release from slavery was obsolete.

"That's the thing." Ryder turned his mug in a slow circle on the table. "I was going to argue the rule still applies because it's built into how the world works, creation, the rhythm of it. Now I think that's the weaker reason, honestly. The stronger one is the slave one. It's not about the universe. It's about people who can't say no to their bosses." He titrated his own certainty as he spoke, adding a little, holding some back. "I'll argue from Deuteronomy. But I have to be honest in the debate that the text disagrees with itself about why, and I don't fully know what to do with that."

Miya picked up the Deuteronomy page and folded it carefully, as if it were hers now. "You're going to lose points for admitting uncertainty," she said.

"I'll lose more if I pretend it isn't there." Ryder reached for the other page, and Marko, still standing at the counter, unread chips in his hand, said quietly, "Then I'd better rewrite my whole case."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In periodized training, a season is divided into cycles; a microcycle, the smallest, usually lasts about one week.
story:
The park at seven in the morning smelled of cut grass and the rain that had stopped an hour before. Dylan sat on the second bench from the fountain with a notebook open on his knees, a pen cap between his teeth, and the strong suspicion that he was doing this wrong. He had written Monday through Sunday down the left margin, then filled every day with something. Sprints, hills, gym, sprints again. Seven days, no gaps, because gaps looked like weakness, and the district trials were in six weeks.

Neil arrived the way Neil always did, juggling a football he had no intention of kicking, his trainers still untimed and unbothered. "You look like a man doing his taxes," he said, dropping onto the bench. Neil wanted one thing and mentioned it roughly every eleven minutes: the last relay spot, the one that had gone to a boy from the other side of town the previous season, when Neil had been a tenth of a second too slow and had told everyone, including himself, that he hadn't really wanted it. He wanted it now.

"Training plan," Dylan said, and turned the notebook so Neil could see. Neil leaned in, still balancing the ball on one finger.

"You've got no rest day," Neil said. "Even I know that, and I once ate a kebab before a timed run."

Dylan knew it too, somewhere under the part of him that believed more was more. Last season, before everything, he had gone eleven days straight and then pulled up lame on the twelfth, a hot wire drawn down the back of his thigh, and he had spent the finals on the grass telling anyone who asked that he was fine. His mother had driven him home with the seat reclined. The physio had said, in the flat tone of a man who had said it four hundred times, that the body adapts during rest, not during work, and Dylan had nodded while thinking about how he would sneak in a session anyway. He hadn't, because he physically couldn't, which was perhaps the only reason the lesson stuck.

"Mr. Goh lent me this," he said, and pulled a worn paperback from his bag, its spine cracked at a chapter near the middle. He had asked the old man about it last week at the courts, expecting a lecture, and Mr. Goh had simply handed over the book and said he could return it when the pages stopped making sense. Dylan had assumed that would take a day. Instead he was on his fourth night, reading on the floor of his room while the rest of the house went dark, and the chapter had a diagram he kept returning to: the season cut into blocks, blocks into weeks, weeks into the smallest unit, ringed and labeled.

Neil took the book, held it at arm's length, and squinted. "There's a word in here you'd like. Microcycle. It's the smallest cycle, about one week." He tapped the diagram. "So your page here, Monday to Sunday, that's one of those. It's got a name. Somebody built a whole vocabulary for this."

"Coaches did, apparently. The season gets divided into cycles, and this is the smallest piece." Dylan looked at his own grid, which suddenly seemed less like a wall of guilt and more like a unit with edges, something you could shape deliberately. He crossed out Saturday, wrote REST, and felt the small heresy of it. Then he wrote WARM-UP above Monday, then above every day, because the physio had also said that, and Dylan had filed it away as something for other people.

Neil was quiet for a moment, which for him was an event, since he was ordinarily loquacious enough that the two of them had once been moved to separate desks in chemistry. "If you're building weeks," he said, "build mine too. The relay spot. I'll do whatever the book says." He said it lightly, but he had stopped juggling the ball, and it sat still on his knee. There was a kind of synchronicity to it, Dylan thought, that Neil would hand him this on the exact morning the plan had started to make sense, though he suspected the word belonged more to coincidence than to fate, and he let it go.

They spent another hour at it, the fountain coughing to life behind them, a dog walker passing twice, the light moving from grey to gold across the wet path. Dylan drew a second column, Neil dictated goals with the book open between them, and they argued amiably about whether Sunday runs counted as rest if you walked the hills. When Neil finally stood, tucked the football under his arm, and jogged off toward the courts without being asked, Dylan stayed on the bench a while longer, copying the week out clean. He still wasn't certain whether rest was strategy or surrender, but the page had a shape now, and he closed the notebook on it and went to find his other shoe.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: Commencement means "beginning"; the word was used for graduation ceremonies because graduates begin a new status, such as being a bachelor or master.
story:
The gown came in a plastic sleeve that smelled like a dry cleaner's, and David hung it on the back of his bedroom door three days before the ceremony so he would stop forgetting it existed. His mother had paid the rental fee without comment, which he understood as a kind of pressure, though he couldn't have said of what. He sat on his bed with the folder of his admission letter, his housing forms, and the essay he was supposed to be revising for a scholarship deadline, and none of it felt like anything he wanted.

At dinner he told his parents he was thinking of skipping graduation. His father looked up from his plate, and his mother said, "You're walking," and that was the whole conversation, so he took his plate to the sink and washed it longer than it needed.

The next afternoon Irene came over with her own gown still in its sleeve, draped over her arm like something she'd shoplifted. She dropped onto the couch in the living room and said, "Yara's skipping. She says it's a pageant for parents."

"It kind of is." David sat in the armchair across from her. "They rent us costumes so they can take pictures."

"It's four hours of your life." Irene pulled her phone out, put it face down on her knee, and looked at him. "What's actually wrong?"

He was quiet long enough that the refrigerator hum filled the room. "Everything ends," he said finally, and it sounded worse out loud, smaller and bigger at the same time. "Yara's going to Seattle, you're going to Montreal. In September I won't know where anyone eats lunch."

"That's the truest thing you've ever said to me." She wasn't mocking him; he could hear the difference. "But you're allowed to be sad about it and still go."

"Why would I want to sit through a ceremony about it?"

Irene turned her phone over, typed something, and read off the screen. "Commencement means beginning. That's why they call it that. It was used for graduation because you begin a new status, like being a bachelor or master." She set the phone down. "It's not a funeral for high school. It's the opposite, apparently. They named the whole thing after starting."

David didn't answer, but he thought about it that night while he packed a box of books he wouldn't need until August. The word had always sounded to him like the machinery of an ending, formal and heavy, the way "conclusion" or "coda" did. He turned his laptop on, half expecting her to have made it up, and found the same thing she'd said: the ceremony was named for the beginning, not the close. It unsettled the shape of the day in his mind, like picking up a stone he'd assumed was attached to the ground and finding it loose in his hand.

On Saturday morning his mother pressed the gown while he stood in the kitchen holding the ironing board steady, and the two of them didn't talk about anything important, which he understood now underpinned most of what mattered between them anyway, the ordinary work of the household carrying what the words didn't. In the car his father drove too slowly, and the school parking lot was full of families taking photographs in the hard noon light.

He found Yara after all, in a gown she must have rented at the last minute, standing near the gymnasium doors and looking embarrassed about being there. "Don't say anything," she said.

"I wasn't going to." But he was glad, a quick, unearned exhilaration that arrived before any thought did, just at seeing that she had come.

The speeches were long, and the air conditioning lost its argument with four hundred gowns, and when his row stood to file toward the stage he watched the graduates ahead of him cross one at a time, each handshake and photograph a small door opening onto whatever came next. He still didn't know whether he was mourning or starting; both felt true, and neither won. Then his name was read out, badly, and he stepped forward into the light.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: Leviticus 19:9-10 commands farmers not to reap the corners of their fields but to leave them, and the fallen gleanings, for the poor and the stranger.
story:
Gavin had claimed the study at his uncle's house because it was the only room with a door that closed, and by eleven on Saturday morning the door had been closed for two hours. His uncle's desk still smelled of pipe tobacco, though nobody had smoked in the house since the funeral. On it lay a photocopied page of Leviticus, a legal pad with three abandoned outlines, and his phone, face down, where Sawyer kept texting: we coming or not.

They came. Sawyer arrived first with a bag of sour candies and the confidence of someone who had already decided what he believed, and Chad followed, carrying nothing, apologizing for being on time. The debate assignment was due Monday: argue whether an ancient religious rule still applied in modern life, using the text itself, no outside scholars, no shortcuts. Gavin had drawn the passage by lot, which was the teacher's phrase for pulling a folded slip out of a coffee mug.

"So it's about farming," Sawyer said, dropping onto the window seat. "Easy. Nobody farms. Rule's dead. We open with that, we're done by lunch." He flicked a candy at the bookshelf.

"Read it first," Gavin said, and slid the page across. "Out loud. I want to hear it."

Sawyer sighed and read. When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap your field to its very edges, nor shall you gather the fallen gleanings of your harvest. You shall leave them for the poor and the stranger. He read it twice, the second time slower, and Gavin watched him arrive at the same place Gavin had arrived at two hours earlier: the moment where a rule about wheat stops being about wheat.

"Okay," Sawyer said. "But I don't own a field. You don't own a field. Chad's afraid of lawns."

"I'm not afraid of them," Chad said quietly. "I just don't maintain one."

Mr. Hassan knocked then, because he was their neighbour and had been their neighbour since the uncle bought the house, and he had never learned not to check on a closed door. He stood in the frame with a plate of his wife's baklava and asked what three boys were doing looking like a jury on a hot Saturday. Gavin explained the assignment, bracing for a lecture, but Mr. Hassan only set the plate down and said he'd argue with anyone about Leviticus after forty years of teaching Sunday school, and then he sat in the corner armchair and said nothing more, which Gavin found more unnouncing than any lecture.

"So what do we argue?" Sawyer said, once the door was shut again. "That it's anachronistic? That's a strong word. Judges like strong words."

"It's not the command that's anachronistic," Chad said, and both of them looked at him, because Chad rarely spoke first. "It's the field. The command is about the edges. About not taking everything. That part doesn't get old." He was picking at the corner of the photocopy without seeming to notice. "My mom's restaurant, they used to pour out the leftovers at closing. Pour them out. Then the new manager started boxing them, and now there's a fridge out back and half the guys from the depot know about it." He shrugged. "Nobody reaps to the corners. Same idea, no wheat."

Gavin wrote that down, then crossed out his three old outlines entirely. "Here's the problem," he said. "The assignment says argue whether it applies. Not kind of, not metaphorically. If I say the rule is really about the spirit and not the field, I've stopped quoting the text and started rewriting it. That's what Mr. Hassan would catch."

From the corner, without opening his eyes, Mr. Hassan said, "Would I."

"Would you," Gavin agreed, and the old man smiled at the ceiling.

They worked through the afternoon. Sawyer, who had walked in ready to declare the whole thing obsolete, spent an hour playing the other side against Chad, and by four o'clock he was arguing that a rule you have to translate out of agriculture before it binds you might bind you less than the farmers it originally bound, since they at least knew exactly where their edges were. Gavin tried to operationalize that, to turn it into something a debate judge could score: if the rule applies, what would a person actually do on Monday morning? Box the leftovers. Leave the margin. But every version he wrote turned on what "the corners" meant, and the text never said, and he kept circling back to the fallen gleanings, the part you didn't even drop on purpose, the part your own carelessness left behind, which somehow still belonged to the stranger.

At six his mother called to say she was picking them up at seven. Gavin had one page left, mostly questions, and he read it aloud once while Sawyer stacked the baklava plate and Chad watched the light go orange across the yard, where his uncle had once let the garden go wild along the fence line because, he'd said once, the rabbits needed it more than he did. Gavin hadn't thought of that in three years.

"Verdict?" Sawyer asked. "Does it apply or not?"

"I think it applies," Gavin said. "I think the field changes and the margin doesn't. But I can't prove the margin is the point, only that it's the part that keeps mattering." He folded the page into his pocket. "We'll open with the text, read it exactly as written, and let the judges decide whether they own a field."

Mr. Hassan stood, brushing crumbs from his trousers, and paused at the door. "For what it's worth," he said, "my congregation has been arguing about that passage since before your father was born." He patted the doorframe once. "You're in good company."

Chad, gathering his jacket, stopped halfway to the door. "I could ask my mom," he said. "About the fridge. If she'd let me take a photo for the debate." He was already pulling out his phone, thumb hovering over her name.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
