knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In the UK, students apply to university through UCAS and can choose up to five courses, listed in no order of preference.
story:
The library's application computers sat in a row by the window, and Naomi had claimed the last one for three hours straight. On the screen was the UCAS site, half-filled, and in her bag was a list of eleven courses she had spent the whole autumn paring down from twenty. The list refused to shrink further. It had become a stubborn thing, like a stain that would not lift, and she read it again now as though a new reading might dissolve one of them.

Zoey dropped into the chair beside her with a stack of prospectuses and a milkshake she was not supposed to have in the building. "Still eleven?"

"Eleven," Naomi said. "Immunology at Edinburgh, immunology at Glasgow, biomedical science at three places, biochemistry at two, one anatomy course, one pharmacology." She flattened the list on the desk. "They're all versions of the same thing. That's the problem. None of them is wrong."

"Then just cut the ones with the worst city," Zoey said, and sucked loudly at her straw.

Naomi almost said that this was a terrible way to choose the next three years of her life. Then she remembered that Zoey had chosen her own A-levels partly because the chemistry labs had better chairs, and that Zoey was, by every measure that mattered, doing fine. There was more than one way to think about the thing. Naomi's mother thought about it in terms of safety: pick the course with the lowest entry requirements, hedge everything. Ms. Aquino, who had taught her biology since year ten, thought about it in terms of appetite: apply where the work would eat you alive in the good way. Naomi had been trying to hold both ideas for weeks, and each time one gained weight the other slid off the scale.

Mohamed-Amine appeared behind them, holding his own laptop like a tray. "Is this the famous list?" He read it upside down, which he could do, a party trick he was proud of. "You know it's five, right?"

"I know it's five." She had known since September, when the form itself told her: five courses, no ranking among them. The form had not told her how to choose, and no ranking meant no ordering of hope either. Edinburgh and her mother's safe pharmacology course would sit on the same list, indistinguishable in weight, and the universities would not even know which one she wanted most. That had bothered her at first, like writing a letter with the paragraphs in the wrong order.

"Five," Mohamed-Amine repeated, tapping the screen where it said so. "Listed in no order of preference. So Edinburgh can sit next to your mum's safety one and nobody sees you flinch."

Zoey raised her eyebrows. "You can choose up to five courses and they don't know which is your favourite? That's actually kind."

"Or dishonest," Naomi said, before she had finished deciding what she thought.

She spent the next hour cutting anyway, because the deadline did not care about her philosophy. She dropped the anatomy course because the modules were mostly things she could take later. She dropped a biomedical science course in a city she had visited once and disliked without being able to say why, which felt like the Zoey method and also felt true. The milkshake migrated between Zoey's hands and Mohamed-Amine's hands. A toddler shrieked somewhere near the picture books and was quietly removed.

The last cut was the worst. She had it down to Edinburgh and one biochemistry course, both good, both wanted, and she sat looking at the two lines while the library's radiator ticked. Her mother's voice said the sensible thing. Ms. Aquino's voice said the hungry thing. Naomi noticed, sitting there, that the two voices had stopped arguing somewhere in the last hour and started instead to agree on a smaller, stranger truth: that she could not rank her own hopes in order either. If someone had forced her to say which of the two she wanted more, she would have guessed, and the guess would have been a performance. The form's indifference to preference was not a flaw she had to compensate for. It was a description of how she actually felt, and she had been resisting it because choosing in no order felt like not choosing at all.

She submitted with five courses, Edinburgh among them, the pharmacology course her mother wanted also among them, sitting side by side, unranked, and then she sat back and waited to feel lighter. She felt approximately the same. Zoey said "congratulations" and Mohamed-Amine shook her hand with mock ceremony, and the milkshake was finished, and outside the window the streetlights came on over the car park.

"You'll find out in March," Zoey said. "Maybe earlier."

"Or later," Naomi said. "It depends."

They packed up. Zoey carried half her prospectuses out of solidarity. At the door, Naomi looked back once at the row of computers, at the machine that now held her five unnumbered choices, holding them all with equal weight, the way a jar holds whatever you put into it.

"So which one do you actually want?" Mohamed-Amine asked, as they stepped into the cold.

"I'll tell you," Naomi said, "when one of them says yes."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
The auditorium piano lived under a gray canvas cover, and Rose had appointed herself its caretaker by showing up every Tuesday after the stage crew cleared out. She had never played anything except three years of reluctant clarinet, which she had abandoned the way you abandon a bad pen, mid-sentence. The piano was different. She wanted it the way you want a language you keep hearing but cannot speak.

Ms. Nwosu, who taught chemistry by day and kept the auditorium keys on a lanyard like a badge of a second, secret profession, had agreed to give her lessons on one condition: Rose practiced on the school instrument, since her family's apartment held a sofa, a table, and no room for even the most apologetic piano. So on Tuesdays Rose arrived early, uncovered the instrument, and waited on the bench while Ms. Nwosu finished whatever paperwork teachers carry like ballast.

It was during one of these waits that Rose began to count. She started with the black keys because they were fewer and looked like a crowd she could manage. She tapped each one with a fingertip, whispering numbers, and arrived at thirty-six, then doubted herself and counted again from the left. Thirty-six, again. The whites took longer, like counting a stadium by rows, and she lost her place twice when Sydney and Delilah came crashing through the side door with a bag of cheese curls.

"Are you doing math on that thing," Sydney said, "or are you playing it very badly on purpose?"

"Eighty-eight," Rose said, mostly to herself. "Fifty-two white and thirty-six black. It adds up. I checked."

"Congratulations," said Delilah, whose acerbic delivery had once made a substitute teacher reconsider her career. "You've discovered arithmetic. Next week, the alphabet."

Rose was about to defend herself when Ms. Nwosu came down the aisle, and the lesson began, and the counting slid to the back of her mind like a coat checked at a door. What stayed in the front was the way her left hand refused to believe her right hand about anything. Her teacher kept saying "trust the shape," which Rose found beautiful and useless in roughly equal measure.

The following Tuesday, Rose tried an experiment she hadn't announced. She had spent the weekend doing what her mother called introspecting, though her mother used the word like an accusation, as if looking inward were a form of truancy. Rose had introspected about the keys. Fifty-two white, thirty-six black, and the odd thing she'd noticed: the black keys came in broken groups, two and three, two and three, all the way up, like a sentence that kept almost rhyming. She had decided the whites were the words and the blacks were the punctuation, or possibly the reverse, and she was prepared to argue either side.

She explained this theory to Sydney and Delilah before the lesson, standing at the edge of the stage with the house lights half up so the auditorium sat in a strange between-glow, neither lit nor dark, a liminality that Delilah said gave her the creeps and Rose privately loved. "The black keys aren't the exception," she said. "They're the map. You find the groups of two and three and you always know where you are."

"That's the stupidest and also smartest thing you've ever said," Sydney offered.

"Both can be true," Rose said. "I've decided to be generous with myself."

When Ms. Nwosu arrived, Rose played the five-finger position she'd been assigned, and then, without permission, played it again starting from a black key, then from another, listening to the strange tilted sound each one made, half familiar and half like a coin landing on its edge. Ms. Nwosu stopped writing in her notebook and watched. Rose knew she was supposed to feel caught, but she felt more like a door had opened onto a hallway she hadn't known the building contained.

"You went off the page," Ms. Nwosu said, which was not praise and not a scolding.

"I went off the white keys," Rose said. "The page was fine."

Delilah, from the third row, cupped her hands around her mouth. "Fifty-two and thirty-six! Don't forget the numbers, genius!"

Ms. Nwosu flipped to a fresh page in the notebook and turned it so Rose could see the blank staff lines waiting there. "Play it again," she said, "the black one, the second one you tried. Slower this time." Rose set her fingers down on the keys.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Guessing a whole number from 1 to 100 by always picking the middle of the remaining range never takes more than seven guesses, which is binary search in game form.
story:
The screen door announced her before she reached the porch, and her grandfather looked up from his chair with the expression of a man who had been waiting specifically to be interrupted. He was convalescing after the hip surgery, propped among cushions with a blanket he kept pushing off, and the whole house smelled of the lemon polish her grandmother wielded like a weapon against boredom.

"You're just in time," he said. "I need an opponent."

"For what?"

"A guessing game. I pick a whole number between one and a hundred. You guess. I tell you higher or lower. First one to find the other's number wins." He held out a legal pad and a pen, as though these were the instruments of a serious contest. "We play until somebody loses three times."

Brooke sat down across from him. Her phone buzzed in her pocket: Gracie, probably, asking whether she'd finished the assignment for Ms. Kamau's class, the one where they had to write code that found a number in a sorted list and then explain, out loud, why anyone would bother doing it a clever way instead of checking every entry one by one. She had been stuck on it for two days. The linear search was easy, almost insultingly easy; the other approach kept slipping out of her hands whenever she tried to type it.

"Fine," she said. "You first. Think of a number."

He thought. She guessed seventy, because it was the middle-ish of everything, and he said lower. Sixty. Lower. Fifty-five. Lower. She noticed, somewhere around her fourth guess, that she was doing something without having decided to do it: each time she cut the remaining range in half, taking the middle of what was left. Forty-two. Higher. Forty-eight. Lower. Forty-five.

"Correct," her grandfather said, and put a tally mark on the legal pad. "Six guesses."

He guessed her number in five. Then it was her turn again, and she found his number in six, and then in seven, and then in four, and across the afternoon the tally marks piled up on her side of the page while his side stayed nearly empty. He lost and lost. Between rounds her grandmother came out with iced tea and stood in the doorway shaking her head at the hydrangeas, muttering that the heat that summer had been pernicious, wilting things at the roots no matter how she watered.

"Ms. Kamau assigned us this exact thing," Brooke said, around the fourth game, feeling her way toward it. "Not the game. The idea behind it. There's a name for it. Binary search. You keep the middle and throw away half." She said it slowly, testing it. "She wants us to prove it's better than going through the list one item at a time, and I couldn't figure out how to say why."

"So say it with numbers," her grandfather said. "How many guesses did you need? Worst one?"

"Seven. I never needed more than seven. Not once, all afternoon."

"And if you'd gone one by one, starting at one?"

She counted in her head. If the number had been a hundred, checking every entry in order, she'd have needed a hundred guesses. The halving had held her under seven every single time. Something assembled itself in her mind, the way a sentence assembles itself before you speak it: the sorted list mattered, because without the order, higher and lower meant nothing, and the halving was only possible when each answer told you which half to discard. On unsorted data the whole method collapsed. She was reaching for her phone to text Gracie when she noticed the legal pad.

Her grandfather had turned it toward himself, and in the margin, in a small careful hand that wasn't his current loose scrawl, were columns of figures. Numbers halved and halved again. A tally of every game, every guess count, every range she'd narrowed. He had been keeping data on her.

"You were counting," she said.

"I was counting," he agreed. He didn't look up. "Old habit. I taught this once, a long time ago, before your mother was born. I wanted to see whether the game still worked the way I remembered."

"The halving?"

"The halving." He turned the pad back toward her so she could see it, forty years of someone else's handwriting suddenly occupying the same page as her tally marks. "The doctors say my memory isn't what it was. They use careful words for it. So I test myself the only way I know how." He tapped the columns. "The method I can still prove. The other thing, the names of things, that part comes and goes, and I'd rather not discuss it at length with my granddaughter on a pleasant afternoon."

Her phone buzzed again, twice. Gracie, then Alisha, then Gracie again, a burst of messages about the assignment, about nobody in the class understanding it, about whether Ms. Kamau would extend the deadline. Brooke typed with her thumb: sorted data matters, always take the middle of what's left, never more than seven guesses for one to a hundred. Then she set the phone face down on the table.

"One more game," she said, and pulled the pad toward her. "This time you guess mine, and I'll count."

He raised his eyebrows, but he folded his hands and said, "Higher or lower?"

She thought of a number and watched his eyes, the small delay before his first guess, and she found she was holding her breath.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: In We Now Know, published in 1997 after Soviet archives had partly opened, Gaddis placed much more responsibility on Stalin personally for the Cold War.
story:
The library closed at nine, and Maxime had until nine tomorrow morning to explain, in eight hundred words, why the same historian had changed his mind about who started the Cold War. He spread the two books across the table like a card trick gone wrong: the older one, thick and dog-eared, that Mr. MacLeod had pressed on him Monday, and the newer one, We Now Know, which Kyleigh had retrieved from the holds shelf an hour ago with the announcement, "Your book is in, and the librarian judged me for my chewing gum."

Kyleigh dropped into the chair across from him and slid the book over. "So what's the actual problem? You look like the books insulted your mom."

"They kind of did. Each other's mom." He opened We Now Know to the pages he'd flagged. "This is Gaddis, right, same guy as the other one. But in here, published in 1997, after Soviet archives had partly opened, he puts way more responsibility on Stalin personally. Like, it's basically Stalin's fault now. The earlier book spread it around more. So my essay is supposed to explain why he changed, and I can't just write 'he found new stuff,' because that's forty words and Mr. MacLeod wants eight hundred."

Kyleigh, who was writing her own essay on something she claimed involved "vibes and the Marshall Plan," leaned over the flags. "Okay, but isn't that the answer? New evidence, new conclusion. Isn't that what scientists do?"

Maxime sat back. In class on Tuesday, Mr. MacLeod had stood at the whiteboard, phlegmatic as ever, and drawn a single wobbly line down the middle. "Resist the urge to dichotomize," he'd said, tapping the line. "The world will offer you two neat boxes. Evidence usually lives somewhere embarrassing in between." At the time Maxime had written it down because it sounded like something that would be on a test. Now the sentence seemed aimed at him personally, across two days and a parking lot.

"Here's what bugs me," he said, pulling a legal pad toward him. "I can't just say the archives proved Stalin did it, because I don't actually know that. Gaddis read the documents; I read Gaddis. He could be overcorrecting. Or the new stuff could be genuinely damning. I've got his old book saying one thing, his new book saying another, and me in the middle with no Russian." He wrote Stalin? with two underlines and then, after a moment, a small question mark after the underlines, which felt honest but looked insane.

Kyleigh stole his pen and drew a arrow between the two books. "So your essay is the arrow. Not the boxes." She pushed the pen back. "That's not a joke, that's actual advice, which is rare for me after six p.m."

He laughed, and then, because it was true, he started writing. Not the essay yet, just a map: the older book's argument in the left margin, We Now Know in the right, and down the center every place where the evidence could be checked, every place where it couldn't, every place where Gaddis himself had flagged uncertainty. Some lines connected. Some just stopped at the spine of one book, unable to cross. He worked for a while without talking, and Kyleigh worked too, or at least held her pen in a working-like posture, and the ceiling fans ticked overhead.

At a quarter to nine the overhead lights blinked twice, the library's version of a throat clearing. Maxime had two pages of arrows and boxes and one sentence he actually liked: that Gaddis's shift was reasonable given what the archives showed, and that Maxime could not independently verify it, and that both things belonged in the essay. It wasn't a conclusion so much as a hand held out toward one. Mr. MacLeod would either accept that or write something dry in the margin. Kyleigh zipped her bag and nodded at his legal pad.

"The arrow, Maxime. Sell the arrow."

He carried both books to the desk, one stacked on the other, the newer one on top.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: TinEye, a reverse image search engine launched in 2008, can sort results with the oldest first, helping find when an image first appeared online.
story:
Dylan had the video open in one tab and the group chat in the other, and his thumb hovered over the forward arrow the way it did when everyone else was still asleep and he could be the first. The clip showed a parking lot swallowed by brown water, a shopping cart drifting past the camera like a small abandoned boat, and the caption said BREAKING: this morning, Route 9. Ninety shares already. Ninety, at seven in the morning, which meant by second period it would be a thousand and by lunch it would be on the local news crawl, and Dylan would have been one of the first ninety.

He had been here before, though, and the memory arrived before the send did. In eighth grade he had forwarded a picture of a burned church with a claim about a town two counties over, and it turned out the photo was from another country entirely, four years old, and a girl in his class had family there and had cried in the bathroom while Dylan sat at his desk feeling the heat crawl up his neck. Nobody had ever traced it to him. That was somehow worse. He had carried it around like a stone in his shoe for three years, and now here he was, thumb hovering, about to test whether anything in him had changed.

"You're doing the face," Melanie said, dropping into the seat beside him. Computer lab, before the bell, the room still smelling of the floor wax the custodian applied at night. Mr. Ma was at his desk at the front, reading something on his phone and pretending not to monitor anyone. "The face where you think you're a detective."

"Where'd you get the flood thing?" Dylan asked.

"Twitter. Why, you don't think it's real?"

Clement leaned across from the next row before Dylan could answer. "I've seen that parking lot. Like actually seen it. And I don't think it flooded this morning, because I drove past it this morning." He tended to pontificate about things like local drainage and highway infrastructure, and usually Dylan tuned it out, but this morning the details snagged. Clement had a long memory for surfaces, for parking lots and storefronts and the exact shade of a chain-link fence. It was his one gift and he deployed it without apology.

"How do you check a picture, though?" Melanie said. "You can't Google a video."

"You can check a frame of it." Dylan wasn't sure where the sentence had come from. He paused the clip where the shopping cart was clearest, took a screenshot, cropped it, and then sat looking at the crop, because the honest truth was he did not know what came next. Mr. Ma, without looking up from his phone, said, "There's a lab account logged in on those machines that has some tools bookmarked. Media literacy unit. Nobody ever clicks them." That was all he said. He went back to his reading as if he had merely mentioned the weather.

The bookmark folder was called Verify, and inside it Dylan found a site he'd never heard of. He uploaded the crop and hit enter. Melanie pulled her chair closer; Clement stood behind them with his arms crossed in a way that looked petulant but was, Dylan knew, just how he watched things. The results loaded as a long column of the same shopping cart, the same brown water, page after page, and at the top of the page was a small sorting menu. Dylan clicked it and chose oldest first, and the column rearranged itself, and there at the very top, stamped with a date, was the photo from years ago. The site had been around since 2008, one of the result pages said somewhere in small print, a reverse image search engine old enough to have watched half the internet's lies be born. Dylan scrolled down the column slowly. Floods in another state. Floods in another decade. The parking lot, dry and ordinary, in a real estate listing.

"So it's fake," Melanie said. She said it flatly, and then her voice went quieter. "I sent it to my group chat. Like twenty people."

"It's not fake exactly," Dylan said, because he found he meant it, and the distinction felt important even as it resisted him. "The flood happened. Just not here, and not now." He was aware of two things pulling at each other: the clean pleasure of catching a lie, which he could feel blooming in his chest like credit, and the muddier fact that the video was real footage of a real disaster that had really ruined someone's parking lot, someone's car, maybe someone's shop. Sharing it had been wrong about Route 9 and right about the world at the same time, and he did not know how to hold both except by saying so out loud.

"I'm going to correct it," Melanie said. "I'm going to reply to myself. God, that's humiliating." She pulled out her phone and started typing, stopped, deleted, started again. Dylan watched her wrestle with it, the little war between pride and the truth, and he thought about the burned church and the girl and how easy it would have been, even then, to type one correcting sentence. He still hadn't decided whether telling her now, telling her everything about eighth grade too, would be honesty or just a way of buying back his own peace. Outside, the bell hadn't rung yet. Mr. Ma turned a page of nothing, still pretending not to listen. Melanie hit send, and the phone made its small, definitive sound.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Between two parallel charged plates, the electric field strength equals the voltage across them divided by the distance between them, written E = V/d.
story:
The gym smelled of floor wax and hot extension cords, and Sara's capacitor sat on the folding table between a volcano that had already erupted twice and Antonin's maze-solving robot. She had built the plates herself, two squares of aluminum foil stretched on picture frames, separated by a gap she had measured eleven times with the calipers Maude lent her. Twelve centimeters. She kept the number in her mouth like a coin.

"Your judge is Weber," Maude said, reading off the clipboard at the check-in table. "She failed my brother's project on optics for spelling."

"She didn't fail it for spelling. He spelled lens wrong nine times."

"Seven. I counted." Maude straightened Sara's sign, which had begun to curl. The sign said nothing Sara trusted anymore. It said "strong field" in Antonin's insouciant handwriting, letters drifting upward as if they had somewhere better to be, and Sara had let it stand because at two in the morning anything printed in marker looked like science.

Antonin came over eating a granola bar that wasn't his. "So explain it to me," he said, which was his way of rehearsing her. "The plates. Go."

"I charge them with the battery, twelve volts, and then there's a field in between."

"What field. Where. Say it like Weber will make you say it."

She looked at the gap between her foil squares, the clean air of it, and felt the old split open inside her, the one between the picture in her head and the numbers on her page. In her head the field was a kind of pressure, something you would feel on your skin if you could fit in there, a wind blowing from the positive plate to the negative one. On her page it was a letter. She had never once made them meet.

"I don't actually know how strong it is," she said. "I know it's there. I know the direction. Positive to negative."

Antonin stopped chewing. "You wrote a whole poster."

"I wrote what the diagram showed. The arrows. I never once asked how big the arrows are."

Maude pulled a stool over and sat down on it backward, arms folded across the back, which meant she was staying. "So find out. You have volts. You have the gap. Twelve volts across twelve centimeters."

"That's it? Just divide?"

"Don't ask me. I spell lens wrong too."

But Sara was already doing it on the back of her hand with Maude's pen, because that was where real arithmetic belonged, and it came out so clean she distrusted it. Twelve volts divided by 0.12 meters. One hundred. One hundred volts per meter, which meant, she thought, that the field pushed with that strength at every point in the gap, and that the size of the arrows had been available to her the whole time, hiding in the two numbers she had been most careful about. She had been guarding them separately like they belonged to different countries.

"Does it work like that?" she said. "Just volts over distance?"

Antonin shrugged with a generosity that let him be wrong. "Judges love a formula. Put it on the sign."

She turned the sign over and wrote it plain, the way she would want it said to her: the electric field strength between two parallel charged plates equals the voltage across them divided by the distance between them, E = V/d. Then, underneath, in her own careful hand, 100 V/m, and she drew one thick arrow from the positive plate to the negative one so nobody, including herself, could forget which way the wind blew.

Ms. Weber arrived at the fourth table of the morning with her clipboard held slightly in front of her, which Sara had watched function all day as deterrence, the way a shield held up makes everyone rehearse their sentences. Up close, though, Weber's eyes went first to the foil, not the sign, and she leaned in to see whether the frames were square.

"Tell me what's happening between your plates," she said.

"There's an electric field," Sara said. "It points from the positive plate to the negative one. Everywhere in the gap, the same strength. And I can tell you how strong, because it's the voltage divided by the distance. Twelve volts across twelve centimeters. A hundred volts per meter." She heard herself say it and glanced at her hand, where the ink was starting to smear.

"You measured the gap yourself?"

"Eleven times. My friend lent me the calipers." Maude, behind her, lifted a hand in acknowledgment without looking up from the robot she was steadying for Antonin, whose project had begun listing to one side.

Ms. Weber wrote something, then paused. "Last week I burned my hand on a soldering iron and the nurse had to cauterize a blister the size of a lentil. That was a hundred watts of something. Your hundred volts per meter, is that dangerous, do you think?"

"I don't think so," Sara said. "It's small. But I don't know where small stops being safe, honestly. That part's not on my poster." Weber looked up at the word honestly, and something in her face loosened, the clipboard dropping an inch.

"Write that down too, then," she said. "The not knowing. It's the part most people leave out." She moved on to the volcano, and Maude came and stood beside Sara, and they watched the foil plates hold their twelve centimeters of charged air between them, invisible, and exactly as strong as arithmetic said.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: The SIFT method from educator Mike Caulfield stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context.
story:
The video arrived in the group chat at eleven at night, and by noon the next day half the grade had seen it: a bridge buckling in grey rain, a voice off camera shouting a city name, the caption promising that this had happened yesterday. Edouard was at Taryn's kitchen table, her laptop open between them, chemistry notes pushed aside. Arnav sat on the counter eating cereal out of the box because Taryn's family, he claimed, kept only turgid whole-grain varieties that absorbed milk like a sponge and weighed a full pound per bite. He leaned over Edouard's shoulder as the clip started its second loop.

"Everyone's resharing it," Taryn said. Her thumb hovered over the forward arrow on her phone. "Even Ms. Vu posted it in the class forum with a sad face."

Edouard didn't touch his phone. Something about the rain looked wrong to him, not dramatically wrong, just slightly off, the way cars in the background had a shape he associated with years he could barely remember. He had read something once, a method with a name, and he chased the memory while Arnav crunched behind him.

"SIFT," he said finally. "My cousin wouldn't shut up about it last summer. It stands for Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, and Trace claims to their original context."

"Stop what?" Arnav said. "We're not doing anything. That's the whole problem with the world, nobody's doing anything."

"Stop before you share," Edouard said. "That's the first part. You just sit there for a second instead of forwarding." He said it flatly, almost embarrassed, but Taryn lowered her phone to the table, and the three of them sat in the loud quiet of a decision not yet made.

The source, when they investigated it, turned out to be an account created three weeks ago that posted exclusively about disasters, each one somewhere different, each one happening "yesterday." Finding better coverage took longer. The mainstream outlets said nothing about any bridge, which either meant the story was too new or not a story, and Edouard had to admit he didn't know which; the absence of evidence, he reminded them, was not the evidence of absence, a line Arnav immediately accused him of stealing from a detective show. It was Taryn who thought of the reverse image search, dragging a frame of the collapsing bridge into the search bar, and the results bloomed across the screen like a family tree, dozens of copies of the same footage, all of them related by a kind of digital consanguinity, every repost descended from one ancestor. The oldest version was dated years ago. The city in the caption wasn't even the city in the original headline. A different country, a different flood, a bridge that had been rebuilt since.

"They recycled it," Taryn said. She said it quietly, as if the video might hear.

"Ms. Vu shared it," Arnav said, and that changed the temperature of the room. It was one thing to catch strangers lying; it was another to watch a teacher they liked pass the lie along. Taryn pulled up the forum thread, seventeen replies deep, people offering prayers for a city that had recovered years ago. She started typing a correction, deleted it, started again. Edouard watched her struggle with the phrasing, the way you had to correct someone without making them feel stupid, which was a skill nobody taught alongside the search-bar tricks.

"Here," he said, and pulled the laptop toward himself. He wrote it plainly: the original date, the original location, the link, no lecture attached. Then, because the words had invigorated him more than he expected, more than the coffee had, he added a single line about running a reverse image search before sharing, so that anyone reading could do the same thing tomorrow with the next video. He hesitated over posting it. He was still not certain about parts of this, about whether the first account had lied knowingly or just lazily, about whether a flood from years ago still deserved the sad face emoji for different reasons. But the date was the date, and the city was the city, and those things could be said cleanly.

Taryn read it over his shoulder and pressed post before he could second-guess it. Arnav slid off the counter, put the cereal box away, and stood behind them as the first reply appeared, a thumbs-up from a classmate Edouard barely knew. Then a second reply, from Ms. Vu: a link to the same original footage, and the words, "Thank you. Deleting mine."

Arnav exhaled slowly, like a man who had been holding his breath through the whole collapse of a bridge. "So we're the fact police now."

"We're one text thread less wrong than we were an hour ago," Taryn said, and closed the laptop, and went to make them sandwiches.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: The derivative of a function at a point equals the slope of the line tangent to its graph at that point.
story:
The bell over the door of Haroon's corner store had a way of announcing people, and Jake had learned to dread it, because most of the time it announced Baby, who did not believe in studying anywhere quiet. Tonight it was worse than usual: Baby came in carrying graph paper, a clear ruler, and a two-liter of orange soda like a trophy.

"Ms. Rivera says if we fail Friday's quiz, she's making us do the whole unit again in summer school," Baby said, laying the paper out on the counter beside the register, over the spot where the scratch-off tickets lived. "So we're doing it here. I already asked Haroon. He said fine as long as we buy something."

Jake turned his worksheet over, as if the answers might be printed on the back. They were not. What was printed was a parabola, y equals negative x squared plus six x, opening downward, and beneath it the instruction: find the maximum using the derivative. He had copied the power rule off the board that morning, brought down the two, and somewhere between the board and the page the whole thing had come apart in his hands. The derivative came out to negative two x plus six, and he had no idea what that had to do with a maximum, or with anything.

Leia slid in beside them with a bag of chips and started reading over his shoulder, which Jake found equal parts helpful and unbearable. "You got the derivative right," she said. "That part's right. It's the next part you're staring at like it insulted your mother."

The fluorescent lights buzzed. Behind them Haroon restocked the cooler, unhurried, occasionally glancing over with the mild, lugubrious patience of a man who had hosted a great many teenagers and their homework and expected to host a great many more.

"Here's my problem," Jake said. He kept his voice low, because the problem felt private, the way not understanding always felt private. "The derivative is a formula. The graph is a picture. They're two different things. Ms. Rivera keeps saying they're connected and then she just points at the board like the pointing explains it." He was aware, even as he said it, that this sounded like complaining, and it was not quite complaining. It was more like standing between two rooms with no door between them.

Baby, who was not taking calculus and considered this a form of wisdom, picked up the ruler anyway. He liked rulers, liked any object with a clear purpose. "What if," he said, and then stopped, because the second half of the sentence had not arrived. He laid the ruler down on the parabola at the point where x was two, tilted it until it looked like it was resting against the curve, and held it there. "Does it look like it's touching right?"

Jake leaned in. At x equals two the curve was climbing steeply, and the ruler, angled to match it, pointed uphill like a ramp. Leia took a pencil and measured: the ruler rose two squares for every one across. "So the slope there is two," she said. "Now do your formula. Negative two times two plus six. That's two."

Jake looked at the number he had computed and the number they had measured, sitting there identical on the page, and felt the door between the rooms open. "Wait. The derivative at a point, that's the slope of the line tangent to the graph at that point. That's what it is. It's not connected to the slope. It is the slope." He said it twice, the second time quieter. He took the ruler from Baby, moved it to the top of the curve, where x was three, and laid it flat against the peak. It sat level, perfectly horizontal, like the horizon out the store's front window, where the streetlights were coming on one by one.

"Zero," Leia said. "Negative two times three plus six is zero. And zero slope is flat, and flat is the top." She said it without triumph, which Jake appreciated, because triumph would have made it hers instead of his.

Baby raised his soda in a small toast. "So the whole test is just putting a ruler on a curve."

"It's not just anything," Jake said, but he said it without heat, because Baby had, in his way, found the door first. Jake had spent a week treating the formula as a kind of magic, symbols that produced other symbols, and Baby had walked in and set a piece of plastic against a drawing. Both were true at once. He was still not certain he could say why the formula and the ruler agreed, only that they did, and that this agreement was either a miracle or the whole point of the subject, and he suspected it was the second thing.

He copied the sketch into his notes, ruler flat on the peak, arrow pointing to x equals three, y equals nine. Haroon drifted over with three coffees nobody had ordered, set them down without comment, and went back to the cooler as if he had done nothing at all.

Jake picked up his pencil again, worked the second problem from scratch, derivative first, ruler second, and when the two agreed he looked up at Leia.

"Ask me another one," he said.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: A buffer in GIS draws a zone of a set distance around a feature, such as every area within 100 meters of a river.
story:
The tent pole kept slipping, and Maika knelt on it with her knee while Mr. Grewal stretched the rainfly over the top. Around the campsite the other students were arguing about who had to carry the water filters down to the creek. She let the argument happen without her. Her laptop was zipped into a dry bag inside her pack, which Leandro had told her was insane to bring on a trip, and which she had brought anyway, because the project was due the Monday after they got back.

The project was flood risk. Mr. Grewal had assigned each of them a city and a question, and hers was simple on its face: who lives in the flood zone? She had the city's official flood layer, a green polygon hugging the river, and she had the housing layer, each parcel a small grey footprint, and where they overlapped the map showed a handful of blocks. A handful. She had sat in the library the week before feeling that the map was lying to her, or that she was lying with it, and she couldn't yet say which.

"Are you actually going to do homework out here," Cash said, dropping onto a log beside her with a bag of trail mix. Dusk was coming down over the creek, and the water, low from a dry summer, made a small patient sound over the stones.

"After dinner," Maika said. "For a bit."

"You're sick," Cash said, but without much judgment, and he flicked a cashew at Leandro, who was testing the camp stove and pretending not to listen.

After dinner, by lantern, she opened the laptop under the tarp Mr. Grewal had strung between two pines. The screen lit her hands blue. She had the flood layer up and the housing layer up, and she stared again at that thin green line and the houses just outside it, the ones her overlay kept excluding. The river ran behind those houses. Their back fences nearly touched the slope down to the water. She knew, the way she knew the smell of her grandmother's street after rain, that a flood did not read polygons.

Leandro crouched under the tarp, ostensibly to get away from the mosquitoes. "What's that doing," he said, nodding at the screen.

"The city says these houses aren't in the flood zone," Maika said. "The river is right there. Like, thirty feet behind them."

"So the map's wrong."

"The map isn't wrong. It's just answering the question they asked it." She said that and then heard it, the way you sometimes hear your own sentence a half second after speaking it. "Or answering it too narrowly."

The tool she hadn't used yet was one Mr. Grewal had demonstrated for about ninety seconds in class before the bell, and she'd written its name in her notebook without understanding it: buffer. She looked it up in the software's help. A buffer, the help said, draws a zone of a set distance around a feature, such as every area within 100 meters of a river. She read the sentence twice, then selected the river, typed 100 into the field, and ran it.

The zone bloomed outward like a slow spill, a translucent band on both banks, and when she layered the housing parcels over it the map changed its mind about everything. The handful of blocks inside the official polygon became whole neighborhoods, three hundred and something homes within a hundred meters of the water, including the row of houses on Delancey Street that she had visited once with her mother, where her mother's friend Rosa lived with her two kids. Rosa's house sat just outside the green. It sat deep inside the buffer.

"Whoa," Leandro said. He had stopped pretending about the mosquitoes. "All those?"

"All those."

Cash had wandered over too, and the three of them looked at the screen while the lantern hissed and somewhere beyond the trees the creek kept up its small sound. Maika turned the layers off and on, off and on, watching families appear and disappear. It frightened her a little, how easy it was. One checkbox made people real to a map or made them nothing. She thought about saying that the tool could reify whatever assumption you fed it, could take an official boundary and hand it back to you as the truth, and she thought about how the word for what she needed instead was something older and less technical: discernment. Not just the power of the software but the judgment about when to use it, and on whose behalf.

She also knew what she couldn't claim. She didn't know whether the city's flood layer already accounted for distance, or elevation, or some model of the water's behavior she had no access to. A hundred meters was a number she'd chosen because the help file used it as an example, not because any engineer had blessed it. She could run it at fifty, at two hundred, and watch the population of the at-risk bloom and shrink, tectonic in its slow rearrangement of who counted. She wrote all of this down in the margin of her notebook, in small letters, because it was the part she'd be honest about on Monday: here is what the tool shows, here is what it can't.

Mr. Grewal came by last, on his rounds before lights out, and stood behind them with his hands in his jacket pockets. He looked at the screen for a long moment, the buffer, the houses, the count in the corner.

"Whose number is that hundred meters," he asked.

"Mine," Maika said. "For now. The help file used it as an example, every area within 100 meters of a river, so I ran it to see. I want to find out what the city uses before I call it anything."

He nodded once, the way he did when an answer was better than the question required. "Leave some room in the write-up for what you don't know yet," he said, and moved on toward the next tarp.

She saved the project twice, to the laptop and the thumb drive, and zipped the dry bag closed. Cash banked the fire down to coals, and the three of them sat for a while not talking, watching the heat bend the air above it. On Monday she would call Rosa's daughter, who was her age, and ask her what the water had done in the yard the spring before last.

"We should put the food in the bear bag," Leandro said, and stood up, holding out the rope.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: In 1859, John Tyndall began laboratory experiments measuring how gases absorb infrared heat, showing that water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb it while nitrogen and oxygen do not.
story:
Nicolas had promised Mr. Greco the report by Friday, and by Thursday night it still consisted of a title, a graph he'd printed from the NOAA website, and a blinking cursor. He sat at the kitchen table with his laptop open beside his mother's unopened mail and a mug of tea gone cold. The graph showed carbon dioxide climbing since 1958, a line that bent upward like a ski jump, and beneath it, in the text he was supposed to summarize, the words "greenhouse gases trap outgoing infrared radiation." He understood the shape of the sentence but not its bones. How did a gas trap anything? Gases slid through cracks under doors. They escaped from balloons.

He texted Gabriella, who was in the other lab section and had already finished her report on ocean plastic. "Do you actually get the greenhouse thing or are you just saying the words," he typed. She replied with a voice memo, four minutes long, which was Gabriella's way. "Okay," she said, "so sunlight comes in, that's visible light, it warms the ground, and the ground gives heat back off as infrared, which is like the kind of heat you feel off a radiator. And some gases catch that on the way out." There was a pause, then, "I think. Don't quote me."

Some gases. Nicolas sat with that phrase the way you sit with a stone in your shoe. If only some gases did it, then the atmosphere wasn't a blanket so much as a room full of people, only some of whom were catching a ball. Which ones? He opened the textbook to the chapter he'd skimmed and found the sentence near the bottom of page 214: in 1859, John Tyndall began laboratory experiments measuring how gases absorb infrared heat, showing that water vapor and carbon dioxide absorb it while nitrogen and oxygen do not. He read it twice. Tyndall, 1859. Before electric lights in houses. Before cars. Nicolas had assumed the whole idea arrived with satellites and supercomputers, some late twentieth-century discovery, and here was a man in a basement with tubes of gas finding it out more than a hundred years before anyone said "climate change" on the news.

On Friday morning Cadence leaned across the aisle before the bell. "You look dour," she said. "Like a monk who lost his flashlight."

"I'm fine. I found out the greenhouse effect is older than my great-great-grandmother."

"Congratulations?"

In class, Mr. Greco called on him first, because Mr. Greco had a memory like a filing cabinet and Nicolas had asked, two weeks ago, whether the report could be handwritten. Now Nicolas stood with his collated pages, the graph clipped to the back, and talked about Tyndall's apparatus instead of the graph. He explained that Tyndall had measured the gases one by one, that water vapor and carbon dioxide absorbed the infrared heat and nitrogen and oxygen let it pass through untouched. "So when you look at the graph," he said, flipping to the last page, "the line going up means more of the catching gas, more heat held near the ground. The experiment and the graph are the same story told a hundred years apart."

"Which gas is doing most of it now?" Mr. Greco asked. Nicolas hesitated. Water vapor, he knew from the textbook, was in some sense the bigger absorber, but the graph in his hand only measured carbon dioxide. The two ideas sat side by side and refused to shake hands. "I'm not sure," he said. "The graph tracks CO2. The atmosphere tracks both. I don't have an instrument that tracks water vapor, so I can't tell you which matters more, only that both work the same way Tyndall showed." A boy in the second row muttered "ascetic monk of uncertainty" and Cadence laughed, and Nicolas found he didn't mind, because the admission had cost him something and he'd paid it.

He had expected Mr. Greco to frown, to press for a tidy conclusion the way rubrics always seemed to want one. Instead Mr. Greco wrote something in his binder and said, "That's a real answer. Most students give me a paragraph of weather forecasts." Walking out, Nicolas caught up with Cadence at the door. "So basically," she said, "a Victorian guy with some tubes started this." "In 1859," Nicolas said, "with nitrogen and oxygen letting everything through." Cadence held the door open with her hip, considering it. "And he didn't even have a graph to worry about. Lucky guy."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: The Taylor rule, proposed by economist John Taylor, says that when inflation rises one percentage point a central bank should raise its interest rate by more than one percentage point.
story:
The economics club met on Thursdays in Mr. Yip's room, which smelled of whiteboard marker and the vending machine nachos someone always smuggled in by three fifteen. Jason had joined in September because it looked tolerable on a college application, and now it was November and he had volunteered, under mild duress, to give the five-minute presentation at the interschool forum on Saturday. His topic: how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. He understood it the way he understood photosynthesis, which is to say he could recite it and draw the arrow diagram and would be helpless if anyone asked a follow-up question.

"Explain it to me," Mika said, sliding into the desk beside him. Mika had opinions about everything and delivered them at a volume calibrated for a room twice the size. "Pretend I'm a judge who hates you."

"Prices go up, so the bank raises rates, so borrowing costs more, so people spend less, so prices stop going up." Jason said it in one breath, the way you'd exhume a dead thing from a shallow grave and hold it up by the tail.

"Convincing," Mika said. "Now the part where you die. If inflation's at six percent, the bank just raises its rate by six points. Match it. Done. Anything more is the bank showing off."

Hope, who sat by the window doing homework for a class she wasn't taking, lowered her pencil. "That's not the rule."

"What rule?"

"The Taylor rule," Hope said. "Proposed by the economist John Taylor. When inflation rises one percentage point, the central bank should raise its interest rate by more than one percentage point." She went back to her homework as though she had recited the weather.

Mika frowned. "More than one. Why more?"

"Because that's the rule," Hope said, which was either the most honest or the least helpful thing anyone had said all afternoon.

Jason wrote it down, and then, because the sentence bothered him the way an untied shoelace bothers a person mid-staircase, he underlined it. More than one. He spent the walk home turning it over, and part of that evening, and a portion of Friday morning he was supposed to give to chemistry. At lunch he cornered Mika again by the salad bar.

"Okay," Jason said. "Say you're right. Say the bank only matches inflation. Rates go up six, inflation goes up six. What did anyone actually feel?"

"A balanced budget of pain," Mika said, taking a roll he hadn't paid attention to selecting.

"Nobody changed anything, though. That's my point. If the bank goes further, goes past the match, then the rate isn't just keeping score. It's actually pushing." Jason heard himself say it and checked, quickly, whether it was true, whether he was arguing or only performing an argument. Both, probably. The honest answer was both.

Mr. Yip found him after last period, tidying a stack of handouts that had been tidied already. "You're the Saturday presenter," he said. "Nervous?"

"A little. Mostly I don't want to be wrong in front of a room."

"That's a reasonable fear and the wrong priority," Mr. Yip said. "You'll be wrong in front of rooms your whole life. Practice being usefully wrong. Say what you know, say what you don't, sit down."

Saturday arrived in the form of a gymnasium at another school, folding chairs, a lectern with a wobble in one leg. Jason watched a girl from the host school give a confident presentation about supply chains and then it was his name being read off a card. He stood at the lectern and adjusted its height twice, which accomplished nothing.

"When prices rise," he said, "the central bank raises its interest rate. And here's the part that took me all week: it raises it by more than inflation rose. If inflation goes up one percentage point, the rate goes up by more than one. That's called the Taylor rule, after the economist John Taylor." He paused. "If you only match inflation, you're a scorekeeper. You have to go past it. The rate has to be higher than inflation, or nothing that anybody does changes." A hand went up in the third row, a boy in a debate-team blazer. "But why more?" the boy asked. "Why exactly more?"

"I don't know," Jason said, and was surprised by the sound of it, how little it cost. "The rule says more. I can tell you what I think it does. I can't tell you why it's that and not something else. Not yet."

Mr. Yip, in the back row, gave him a small nod that could have meant anything. During the Q&A the debate boy came back twice more, once with a question about profligate government spending, which Jason fumbled, and once with a question about whether central bankers ever get it wrong, which Jason answered with "constantly," getting the room's only laugh. Afterward, Mika found him by the juice table.

"You admitted you didn't know something," Mika said. "In public. Bold."

"It was either that or invent a mechanism on the spot."

"Counterpoint," Mika said, filling a cup, "inventing mechanisms on the spot is a life skill. Ask any adult."

Hope appeared with her coat already on. "You said 'more than one' four times," she said. "By the fourth time the blazer kid believed you. I watched it happen." She pulled her scarf tighter. "Same bus as me?"

Jason looked at the empty lectern, still wobbling faintly whenever someone brushed past it, and then at the door. "Yeah," he said, and picked up his bag.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Sociologist Ray Oldenburg's 1989 book The Great Good Place named 'third places', such as cafes and libraries, where people meet outside home and work.
story:
The truck's passenger seat had a crack across it that Logan kept his thumb in while the highway poured past. His father drove with both hands at ten and two, careful the way he was careful about everything now, and behind them, in Reilly's dented Civic, came the last of the boxes. Reilly had insisted on following the truck the whole two hundred miles, though he was only staying one night before driving back.

"You didn't have to come," Logan said.

"I know."

Reilly's want had never been subtle. He wanted a promise. All summer he had been circling it, saying things like it's not like you're dying and we can do this every month, and at the going-away party Kelly-Anne had cornered Logan by the fence and said, "He needs you to say you'll come back. Just say it, whether you mean it." Logan had said he'd think about it, which had made the music inside seem very loud for a minute.

They stopped at a library in a town whose name Logan forgot immediately, because his father needed to rest his eyes and because Logan needed to use a bathroom that wasn't a gas station. The library was cool and smelled like carpet glue and old paper. Two women were shelving books near the front, and an older one, whose name tag said Nolan, was arguing gently with the other about where a sociology section ought to live.

"It's not fiction, it belongs with the social sciences," Ms. Nolan said. She held up a thin paperback. "Oldenburg, The Great Good Place, 1989. He called them third places. Cafes, libraries, the spots where people meet outside home and work. First place home, second place work, third place everything that matters in between."

Logan stood near the new arrivals shelf pretending to read spines. He had never heard the phrase before, but he recognized the shape of it instantly, the way you recognize a face before a name. The skate shop where he and Reilly and Kelly-Anne had spent every Saturday since tenth grade, drinking flat whites they didn't like because the sitting was free. The bleachers behind the field where nothing official ever happened. Nobody had planned those places. They had just accreted, the way Reilly said river stones did, and now Logan was being lifted out of the river entirely.

Back in the truck, his father pulled onto the on-ramp and said, "Find anything good in there?"

"A book," Logan said. "Sort of a theory."

"Mm," his father said, which was his whole vocabulary for the theoretical.

At the new house Reilly carried boxes badly and made jokes about the wallpaper until dark, and then they sat on the porch steps with the last two sodas from the cooler. The street was quiet in a way that felt subterranean, like the silence had been buried under the town and had risen up through the soil. Somewhere a dog barked twice and stopped, embarrassed.

"So," Reilly said. "You'll come back. Thanksgiving, Christmas, some weekends."

Logan turned the can in his hands. He had spent the last two hundred miles trying to exhume his own position from the rubble of politeness and fear, and what he had dug out was this: he did not know yet whether a friendship could survive on scheduled visits, and he did not know whether it could survive on nothing, either. He thought of the library table he was already planning to claim, the same table every afternoon until the faces around it stopped being strangers, and he understood that he was about to do deliberately, over months, what had happened with Reilly by accident, over years. That felt less like betrayal than like arithmetic, though he couldn't have said why.

"I'm not going to promise a schedule," Logan said.

"Wow."

"I'm going to text you every day. And when there's a real reason, I'll drive back. Kelly-Anne's graduation. Your dad's thing."

"My dad's thing," Reilly repeated, flat.

"But listen." Logan told him about the book, about third places, about how he'd been walking around all day feeling like the problem was that he'd left, and maybe the problem was narrower than that. Maybe he'd left a place, and places could be built. "It won't be the same one," he said. "It'll be a different one. That's all I've got."

Reilly drank the last of his soda and crushed the can against his knee. He looked down the dark street at the house across the way, where a light went off in an upstairs window. "Every day," he said.

"Every day."

"You say that now."

Logan stood and stacked the empty cans. Through the window he could see his father in the kitchen, unpacking a single box labeled DISHES, setting plates on a shelf one at a time, checking each against the one before it.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Cocoa butter can crystallize in six different forms, and tempering aims to make most of it set in form V, the crystal form that gives shine and snap.
story:
The chocolate had failed twice, and Mackenzie was beginning to take it personally. She stood in her grandmother's kitchen with a bowl of grey, streaky chocolate that had set overnight into something that looked like old candle wax, and she broke off a corner. It didn't snap. It bent, then crumbled, and her tongue found a texture like wet sand. Her grandmother had gone to bed an hour ago, leaving Mackenzie the good saucepan and a warning not to burn anything, which Mackenzie had honored, technically. The chocolate had never burned. It had simply, quietly, ruined itself.

She texted Darwin a photo of the broken piece with the caption "attempt two." He replied with a thumbs up and nothing else, which was his way of saying he was at his cousin's and useless. Chelsea, who was still awake at eleven because Chelsea was always awake at eleven, sent back a screenshot from some chocolate-making forum, and underneath it: "read this it's about crystals."

Mackenzie read it twice. Cocoa butter, the forum said, in a post written by someone named ChocolatierLars, could crystallize in six different forms, and only one of them, form V, gave you shine and that clean snap. Her grandmother's kitchen was quiet except for the fridge humming, and Mackenzie sat on the counter with her phone held close to her face, reading the sentence over and over. Six forms. She had imagined chocolate as a thing that either worked or didn't, a coin flip she was losing, and it was a relief to find out the coin had six sides. The other forms, the post implied, were the dull ones, the crumbly ones, the ones that had colonized her bowl overnight like squatters in an empty house.

She found her grandmother's candy thermometer in the second drawer, behind a morass of rubber bands, expired coupons, and a single knitting needle whose partner had presumably died. The thermometer looked older than the house. She resuscitated it anyway, washing off a decade of dust, and clipped it to the saucepan, and chopped the last of the good chocolate into small even pieces the way the forum said, because small pieces melted evenly and evenness, apparently, was everything now.

The technique was called tempering, though Chelsea's screenshot called it "playing seed the crystal," which sounded like a band name. You melted the chocolate hot, then cooled it while stirring, then warmed it again slightly, keeping it in a narrow range, because the crystals were competitive and form V was the one you wanted to win. Mackenzie understood it the way she understood her chemistry unit on saturated solutions, which was to say she could follow the steps without being able to say exactly why the universe had arranged itself this way. She stirred. The chocolate went glossy and thin, then thickened as it cooled, and she kept stirring until her wrist ached, watching the thermometer like it owed her money.

Ms. Gagnon from next door knocked at the back door at half past midnight, which was later than neighbors usually knocked, but Ms. Gagnon was ninety-one and had never observed a boundary she couldn't gently cross. "Your light's on," she said. "I thought it was burglars, but burglars don't smell like that." She came in without being invited, which was also standard, and stood at Mackenzie's shoulder while Mackenzie stirred.

"Grandmother taught you?"

"I'm teaching myself. It's not going well."

"It never did go well for her," Ms. Gagnon said. "Sixty years in this kitchen and her chocolate was always dull. She blamed the saucepan."

"It's not the saucepan." Mackenzie lifted the thermometer to check it. "It's the crystals. Cocoa butter can set in six different forms, and only one of them, form V, gives you the shine and the snap. Everything else is crumbly." Saying it out loud, she realized she believed it, fully, in the way you only believe a fact once you've ruined two batches against it.

Ms. Gagnon lowered herself onto a kitchen chair and watched. "So you're steering it."

"I'm trying." The chocolate had cooled to where the forum said to warm it back up, and Mackenzie moved the bowl over the pan for three seconds, then off, then on again for two, stirring the whole time. Her nascent confidence rose with the temperature, and she knew enough now to distrust that too, because the window was narrow and the forms were patient. She could do everything right and still not know, until it set, whether she'd done anything at all. She spread a spoonful of the chocolate on waxed paper and put it in the fridge's coolest corner, and the three of them, in the fluorescent hush, watched the timer count down five minutes.

The test strip came out shiny. Mackenzie held it up to the light and it gleamed like a new coin, and when she broke it, it snapped, a clean bright sound in the quiet kitchen, and Ms. Gagnon said, "Well," and nothing more. Mackenzie stood there holding the two halves, and outside the window the yard was black and the streetlight made one pale circle on the grass, and she thought of the whole batch still waiting in the bowl, and of her grandmother asleep down the hall with sixty years of dull chocolate behind her, and she picked up the spatula and started spreading.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Kwanzaa, created by Maulana Karenga in 1966, runs from December 26 to January 1 and honors seven principles, one each day, beginning with Umoja, meaning unity.
story:
The kinara had been in the hall closet for three years, wrapped in a dish towel, and Matthew's mother set it on the table between the bowl of fruit and the stacked presents nobody was allowed to touch until after dinner. It was December 26, the first night, and the house smelled of collards and cornbread drifting in from the kitchen where his grandmother ruled with a wooden spoon. Matthew had been assigned the candle and the explanation, and he stood at the table rehearsing under his breath while his little cousins chased each other around the couch.

The trouble was that he had not rehearsed enough. His mother had handed him a photocopied page a week ago, told him to know it by tonight, and he had read it once in the car, once in the bathroom, and then his mind had gone soft and lazy on the details. He remembered the shape of the thing but not its numbers, and now his grandfather was already lowering himself into the chair at the head of the table, waiting.

His cousin Maxime slid in beside him and whispered, "You good?"

"I'm good," Matthew said, which was not true, and Maxime knew it was not true, because Maxime had watched him read the page upside down in the car and could probably recite more of it than he could.

The family settled. Grandmother brought out the red candles, then the green, then the single black one for the center, and his mother nodded at Matthew to begin. He lit the black candle, and its flame wavered in the draft from the kitchen.

"Kwanzaa was created by Maulana Karenga," he said, "in 1966." He was glad that part had stuck, because his grandfather's eyebrows had lifted at his first pause. "It runs from December 26 to January 1, and it honors seven principles, one each day." He took a breath. "And today's the first day, so today's principle is..." He looked at the candle as if it might whisper to him. Nothing came.

"Umoja," said his aunt from the doorway, drying her hands on a towel. "It means unity."

"Umoja," Matthew repeated. "Unity." His face was hot, but nobody laughed, and his grandfather tapped the table once, which was his way of saying go on.

So he went on, though the going was harder now. He said that unity meant the family at this table, the neighborhood around the block, and he heard, even as he said it, how close he was drifting to the tautological, unity meaning we should be unified, which his father would have called saying nothing twice. He tried again. He said unity meant his grandmother and her sister speaking on the phone every Sunday for forty years even through the years they were angry, and that was better, that was something with a face on it, and Maxime nodded at him across the table.

Later, while the food went around and the little ones were told twice to wash their hands, Maxime pulled him into the hallway. "I need you to cover for me," Maxime said. "After dinner. I'm going out."

"On the first night?"

"That's the point." Maxime's jaw was set the way it got during arguments with his own mother, who lived two streets over and had not come tonight, which everyone knew and no one had said aloud. "Nobody will notice if I leave after the candle. You're up there talking about unity and half this family didn't come. Uncle Russell's in Cincinnati. Auntie Dee didn't even call." He gestured at the living room full of people, and Matthew understood that what Maxime wanted was not to escape the celebration but to prove something about the family that had failed to gather, to make the absence visible by adding himself to it.

"Leaving doesn't show them anything," Matthew said. "It just makes the table smaller."

"Everything I do makes the table smaller, according to your mom."

Matthew looked back through the doorway. His grandfather was laughing at something, his whole chest involved, and his mother was refilling glasses without being asked. He thought about his own fumbling at the candle, the way his aunt had caught him and passed the word to him without shaming him, one hand under another. He did not have a clean answer for Maxime, and he was tired of pretending he did.

"Stay for the karamu," he said instead. "Eat, do the gifts, and then if you still want to go, I won't say anything. One night, most of it." It was a compromise that satisfied nobody fully, which was maybe the only kind that held.

Maxime studied him for a long moment, arms folded, and then his shoulders dropped a fraction. "Fine. Most of it."

They went back in together. Grandmother was ladling out the stew, and she pointed her spoon at the two empty chairs side by side and said, "Sit. And somebody tell me again what that word was."

"Umoja," said Matthew. "It means unity."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: The legal age of consent differs by country and even between US states, and in many places it falls between 16 and 18.
story:
Kaitlyn had expected the clinic to smell like fear, but it smelled like hand sanitizer, the kind that desiccated the skin of her knuckles within a minute and left them pale and tight. She stood at the reception window with her volunteer badge pinned crooked to her jacket and asked, for the third time, whether she was supposed to be in the back room or the front.

"Back room," the receptionist said without looking up. "Ms. Brennan called ahead. You're the peer educator from the high school."

The back room was a strip of corridor with three folding chairs and a rack of pamphlets, and Kaitlyn's job, according to the laminated sheet Ms. Brennan had given her, was to sit with patients before the doctor saw them and explain, in plain words, what they could ask for: contraception, testing for infections, and, if they wanted it, someone to talk to about consent. She had practiced on Audrey-Ann over milkshakes, and Audrey-Ann had laughed and said, "You sound like a pamphlet yourself," which had stung more than Audrey-Ann meant it to.

The morning passed slowly until Hannah came in.

Hannah sat in the middle chair with her sleeves pulled over her hands, and she did not say hello. She said, "I don't even know if I need to be here."

"That's okay," Kaitlyn said. "You don't have to know. Do you want to tell me what happened, or do you want me to just walk you through what they can do?"

Hannah was quiet long enough that Kaitlyn counted the tiles on the floor. "There was a guy," Hannah said finally. "From the state school. I turned seventeen in March and he's eighteen, and my mom found out and now she's saying he broke the law, and I'm saying he didn't, and nobody will tell me who's right."

Kaitlyn's stomach dropped, not because she didn't know anything, but because she knew just enough to know she didn't know enough. She remembered the summer at her grandmother's house, sitting at the kitchen table with the fan pushing hot air around, reading a news story on her phone about a law in another country. She had read it twice and then said, out loud, "That's not what it is here," and her grandmother, who was sorting annuity statements into folders, had said, "Different places, different rules, honey. That's true of everything, not just that." Kaitlyn had assumed the difference was between countries. It had not occurred to her, until this moment, that it could differ between states, that crossing a county line might change what counted.

"Okay," she said slowly, pulling out her phone. "I'm not going to guess at you. Let me look it up."

"Whatever," Hannah said, but she leaned over.

The search took four minutes, and the answer was not one answer. The legal age of consent differed from country to country and even between states, and in many places it fell between sixteen and eighteen. Their own state was on one side of that range, the neighboring state on the other, and Hannah's guy, technically, lived in neither.

"So it's different everywhere?" Hannah said. "Like, in some places sixteen counts and in some places you have to be eighteen, and in some it's in between?"

"That's what it looks like," Kaitlyn said. "But Hannah, I have to be honest with you. I don't know all the details, like how close in age people have to be or how any of this actually gets decided. I can tell you what the page says and that's it. I'm not a lawyer. Neither is your mom, probably."

"She's not," Hannah said, and for the first time she almost smiled.

Kaitlyn set the phone down on her knee. "Can I tell you what I actually know something about? The doctor here can test you for infections, and it's confidential, and she can talk to you about contraception. And if something happened that you didn't want, even if it's legal, even if nobody broke a law, you can still say that out loud here and someone will listen. Legal and okay aren't the same thing."

Hannah looked at her sleeves. "He didn't make me do anything. That's not it. It's just my mom thinks one thing and I think another and I wanted somebody to tell me who was right."

"Nobody's going to be able to tell you that today," Kaitlyn said. "I'm sorry. I can tell you the doctor's good, and the tests are quick, and you don't have to decide about your mom."

The nurse called Hannah's name, and Hannah stood up, and at the door she turned around. "You didn't sound like a pamphlet," she said. "Audrey-Ann said you would, but you didn't."

Afterward Kaitlyn sat in the folding chair and reapplied nothing to her ruined knuckles, and thought about how strange it was that the summer had already hardened into something fixed, like rock, when it had felt metamorphic at the time, hot and shifting, and she had liked it that way. She texted Ms. Brennan a report, deleted the part where she admitted she'd had to look everything up, typed it back in, and sent it.

"Hannah left a few minutes ago," the receptionist called back through the window. "She said to tell you she'd text you about Tuesday."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: A home with a 1 percent yearly flood chance has about a 26 percent chance of flooding at least once during a 30-year mortgage.
story:
Alexandra saved her map project to the library's shared drive, sat back, and waited for the lab computers to stop whirring. On her screen, the city sat in two layers: the hundred-year floodplain in translucent blue, and the housing parcels in faint orange. Where the layers overlapped, the color turned a muddy green, and the green ran through the east side like a stain.

"I don't get what you're doing," Carla said, pulling the spare chair over. "Isn't this Ms. Goh's thing? Extra credit?"

"It was extra credit. Now it's a favor for my aunt's friend." Alexandra zoomed to the river bend. "He's closing on a house Friday. Two streets from the water. He keeps saying it's never flooded, so it's fine."

Carla leaned in. "Has it?"

"Not in the twenty years he's lived around here. That's what he says." Alexandra clicked the attribute table for his parcel and the number came up: one percent annual chance. "The map calls his lot one percent yearly flood chance. He thinks that means it basically can't happen. Like one in a hundred, every year, forever, so why worry."

Paxton arrived with a printout of mortgage rates and set it beside the keyboard, because he had opinions about rates and no place to put them. "Thirty-year fixed," he said. "That's what he'd get. What's the flood number?"

Alexandra did the arithmetic in the margin of Paxton's printout, compounding the yearly chance across the years of the loan, and then did it again because the result annoyed her.
