Across thirty years, the one percent added up to about a twenty-six percent chance of flooding at least once before the mortgage was paid off. She wrote 26% and circled it. "That's more than one in four," she said. "For one flood. At least one."

Paxton whistled. Carla frowned at the screen as if it had lied to her.

Ms. Goh came by on her rounds, saw the circled number, and asked only whether Alexandra trusted her layers. That was the right question, it turned out. Alexandra opened the metadata panel and found the flood layer was a state draft from years before the city redrew the drainage upstream, and the housing layer came from the county assessor, whose parcel lines disagreed with the city's by a few meters in exactly the green band she cared about. Provenance, the panel called it, and Alexandra had skipped it until now. She had assumed the map was the ground. It was a document with authors.

So she spent an hour interposing a third layer, the city's corrected stormwater data, between the two, and the muddy green around the family friend's street thinned. His parcel sat at the edge of the one percent zone, half in, half out, depending on whose parcel lines you believed. The twenty-six percent over thirty years was still true for the one percent itself, she was sure of that much. Whether his house carried that one percent was the uncertain part, and the map would not settle it by Friday.

Carla had been quiet, scrolling the east side. "You know what's parochial about this," she said. "Everyone argues about that one street near the river. Look at the green across the whole neighborhood. Half those people rent. Nobody's making them a spreadsheet."

Alexandra looked. The overlay showed what she had not thought to look for: the deepest green sat over rental blocks and two apartment buildings, not over the riverfront streets with the nice porches. Her errand for her aunt's friend, one man with a mortgage and a choice, had been the smallest problem on the screen. She had wanted a clean answer, a number she could carry to him, and instead she had a number attached to an unresolved boundary.

She emailed the family friend anyway: the one percent yearly chance, the twenty-six percent chance over a thirty-year mortgage, and a note that the parcel sat on the edge of the zone and he should pay for a survey and check the drainage maps at city hall before Friday. Then she opened a new file and titled it East Side Rentals, and pulled the parcel layer down over the corrected floodplain.

"That's not due for Ms. Goh," Carla said.

"No," Alexandra said, and dragged the boundary of the study area east, past the river bend, past his street, to where the green was darkest. Paxton slid his chair over and started counting addresses.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Research by linguist Paul Nation and colleagues suggests readers need to know about 98 percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help.
story:
The festival had taken over the school gymnasium, folding tables draped in cloth from a dozen countries, the air thick with fried dough and cardamom. Grayson had come for extra credit, which Ms. Ahmadi offered to anyone who could read a short news article in a language they were studying and summarise it aloud at the Persian table. He had been learning Farsi for eight months, mostly at night, in the blue boreal glow of his laptop, and he had picked an article that morning from a Tehran paper, printed it, and told himself it would be fine.

It was not fine. The first paragraph contained at least nine words he did not know, and the second paragraph contained more, and by the third he was doing what he always did, which was guessing, retrofitting the sentence around whatever verbs he recognised. He sat behind the Persian table with the paper flattened under both hands while Hamzah, who had come along purely for the food, leaned over his shoulder.

"You look like you're defusing something," Hamzah said.

"In a way." Grayson tapped a word with two syllables that refused to resolve into anything. "Every paragraph feels like a puzzle where I've lost half the pieces."

Hamzah's older sister studied linguistics, and Hamzah, who absorbed her dinner conversation the way other people absorbed television, frowned at the page. "She talks about this. There's research by this guy, Paul Nation, and other people who work with him. Readers need to know about ninety-eight percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help. Ninety-eight. Like, almost all of them." He said it the way he reported most things, with the mild surprise of someone who had never checked the math himself. "You probably know, what, eighty?"

Grayson counted the first line. Sixteen words, four unknown. He did the arithmetic in the margin, feeling the number land somewhere short, and understood for the first time why the article had felt less like reading and more like decoding, why each sentence demanded negotiation before it would yield. Ms. Ahmadi was across the gym, explaining the haft-sin table to a cluster of freshmen. He had maybe twenty minutes before his turn.

He could pick an easier article. There was a stack of them at the table, children's news, simplified digests, and choosing one would have been the practical thing. But the article he had chosen was about a village in the north that had restored an old orchard, and it was the reason he had started learning the language at all, because his grandmother had been born in a village like that and had never taught anyone her words, taking them with her when she died two winters ago. Switching to a simplified digest felt like a small casuistry, a bargain in which he told himself he had honoured her while actually honouring his grade.

So he compromised, though he knew it was a compromise. He went through the article with a dictionary and marked every unknown word, translating them in the margins until the page looked annotated like a legal brief, and when Ms. Ahmadi called him up to the microphone he carried it with him, intending to glance down only when stranded.

He read haltingly. The words he had just learned came out stiff, without music, and the words he had known for months carried the sentences between them. When he reached the end, he closed the paper and summarised aloud, in Farsi, that a village near the Caspian had replanted an orchard older than the mosque, and that the oldest resident, a woman of ninety-three, had wept when the first trees fruited. His summary was shorter and plainer than the article. He could hear everything the language had wanted to say that he could not repeat, the way a photograph shows you what stood outside the frame.

Ms. Ahmadi applauded with the small crowd, then came over while he was coiling the microphone cord. "How long have you been studying?" she asked, in English.

"Eight months."

She looked at the article, at his crowded margins, and said nothing about the difficulty, which he understood was its own kind of verdict. Then she said something he did not expect. "The woman in the article. Ninety-three. Her name was Ashraf Derayati." She watched his face. "Your grandmother. You told the class, in September, that she was from near Rasht. I read that piece when it came out. I wrote to the paper about it, actually, years ago. They ran a small feature on the orchard's restoration, and the family was mentioned."

He held the cord still in his hands. He wanted to ask which family, which names, whether anyone remained, whether a letter could be sent, whether the orchard still stood, and he could feel the questions crowding his mouth in two languages, only some of which he had the words for. Ms. Ahmadi seemed to know it. She said, "When you can read the whole article without marking the margins, you could write to them yourself. That kind of thing, if it goes well, could augur something. Or it could go nowhere. Letters to villages often do."

Hamzah appeared at his elbow with two paper plates of food, holding one out. "So did we pass?"

Grayson took the plate. Behind them the microphone passed to a girl reading Korean, her voice easy and unbroken, and he folded his marked-up article along its worn creases and put it in his back pocket, planning already to read it again tomorrow, and the day after, until the margins were empty.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: In his 1963 book The Making of the English Working Class, E. P. Thompson said he wanted to rescue ordinary workers from 'the enormous condescension of posterity'.
story:
Nathan spread the microfilm printouts across the library table like evidence at a trial nobody was attending. He had started the whole project three weeks ago, when his grandmother handed him a shoebox and said, "Your great-great-grandfather worked in a mill, and that's all anyone remembers," and something about the phrase all anyone remembers had stuck in him like a splinter.

"Chemistry still due tonight," Lyndon said, dropping into the chair across from him. He slid his lab notebook over the printouts. "You were supposed to help me titrate the vinegar thing. I need someone to watch the flask while I record."

"In a minute." Nathan held up a page, a census scan so faint the ink looked like water damage. "Look at this. 1891, Halifax. Jonah Platt, spinner. That's him. Then I searched every mill history in this building, and he's not in one of them. Not one."

"Because he was a spinner," Lyndon said, as if this were obvious. "Nobody writes books about the guy who died before anything interesting happened to him." He set up the burette between two stacks of local history and opened his textbook to the enthalpy problem, sighing at it the way you sigh at a friend who always borrows money.

Ms. Krause came by with the trolley, paused, and read the upside-down census page. "If you want the mill workers," she said, "you're in the wrong section. Try 942 over there, the social history shelf. Though I'll warn you, two of those books argue with each other the whole way through. It's like listening to my uncles at Christmas." She pushed the trolley on before Nathan could ask what she meant.

He found the shelf. One book, thick and orange, was by a man named E. P. Thompson, and when Nathan flipped to the preface, dated 1963, he stopped reading normally and started reading the way you read a letter addressed to someone else that turns out to be about you. In his book The Making of the English Working Class, Thompson wrote that he wanted to rescue ordinary workers from "the enormous condescension of posterity." Nathan copied the phrase onto his hand because his notebook was under Lyndon's flask.

"Listen to this," he said, coming back to the table. "There's a historian who wrote a whole book because he thought people like Jonah got looked down on by, basically, us. By later people. The enormous condescension of posterity. That's the actual phrase."

"That's a band name," said Matias, who had arrived late, as arranged, carrying the vending machine snacks. He peeled an orange. "So one guy wrote a book. So what? You said the other book argues with him."

"It does. Sort of. The other one says the mills modernized the region, gives all these output figures, and the workers barely appear except as hands." Nathan sat down. "But here's the thing. When Thompson wrote, in 1963, he was asking why ordinary workers weren't in the story. The other guy was asking why the economy grew. Different question, different book. It's not that one of them is lying."

Lyndon titrated the last of the vinegar solution, watching the color change in the flask the way Nathan was now watching the two histories, adjusting one drop at a time. "So which one do you believe?"

"I did believe the first one I read," Nathan said. "I was furious at the mill owner for about an hour. Then I read the second and thought, well, the output figures are real too, people's lives got longer, that's not nothing." He turned the census page toward the window light; the paper's surface had gone friable at the edges, and a corner crumbled off under his thumb, dusting the table. He caught the fragment before it slid into Lyndon's beaker. "The sources are partial. Mostly what got saved is what owners and magistrates wrote down. Jonah's in a census because the government counted him, and then he's gone."

"So your essay says what?" Matias asked, working a segment of orange loose.

"I don't know yet. Something like: history isn't one story that got told wrong, it's a bunch of stories that got told for different reasons, and the reasons changed." Nathan stacked the printouts, then unstacked them, because the order he'd chosen assumed an ending he hadn't earned. "I might be wrong about half of it. I'm keeping that part in."

The library speaker announced closing in fifteen minutes. Lyndon capped the burette, and Ms. Krause passed their table again on her final round, glancing at the Thompson book lying open on the census scan, Jonah's name and the enormous condescension of posterity touching along the page break like two people introduced at a party. "You're not checking that out?" she said.

"I'm coming back tomorrow," Nathan said, and slid the book into the gap between 942.084 and 942.085, spine out, exactly where he'd be able to find it.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: Capitalization means unpaid interest is added to a loan's principal, so from then on interest is charged on the interest too.
story:
Evan's sister had asked him to come along because she didn't trust herself not to cry at the counter, and he hadn't argued, because he wanted to see the number himself. She'd said it on the drive over, gripping the wheel at a red light: she'd borrowed twenty-six thousand dollars, and the balance on her statement said more than that, even though she'd been paying interest all along, or thought she had. The credit union smelled like carpet cleaner and coffee that had sat too long. They took a number, and she sat with the statement folded into smaller and smaller squares in her fist.

Luc was working the desk by the savings windows, and he waved them over before their number came up. Luc had been in Evan's grade until he'd deferred a year to work here, and he'd grown into the job the way other people grew into uniforms, comfortable and slightly formal at once. He read the statement once, then again, and clicked through something on his screen.

"It's called capitalization," he said. "The interest you weren't paying got added to the principal, so now they charge interest on the interest too." He said it flatly, without apology, the way he'd announce a branch holiday.

"Nobody told me that," his sister said.

"It's in the paperwork." Luc turned the monitor toward her a few degrees, then thought better of it and turned it back. "You deferred the payments. The interest didn't defer anything."

Evan stood slightly apart, watching his sister's face do several small things in sequence, and found himself unexpectedly angry at her, which he then felt guilty about, because it wasn't her fault, exactly, or maybe it was entirely her fault, and neither conclusion held still long enough to be useful.

Mr. Nolan, who had coached Evan in track two springs ago and now handled loans at the far counter, came over with two waters from the cooler. He set them down without ceremony, like a man setting out hurdles. "There are options," he said. "Income-driven plans. Consolidation. Some of it depends on when the interest capitalized and how the servicer applied your early payments." He had the acerbic manner Evan remembered from the track, sharp with slow runners and unfailingly patient with the ones who showed up on Saturdays, and it was the patient version he was using now.

While his sister went through the numbers with Mr. Nolan, Evan drifted back to Luc's desk. On the counter was a stack of brochures about certificates and savings accounts, and he picked one up mostly to have something in his hands. There was a chart in it, a line crawling upward at a slow bend, and beneath the chart a word he recognized from chemistry: growth, compounding. "So savings do this in reverse," he said.

"Sort of the mirror image," Luc said. "Interest gets added, and then you earn on what was added. Same machinery, pointed the other way." He straightened the brochure stack. "People get emotional about which side of it they're standing on."

Evan thought of his sister, who had borrowed because nobody in their family had the money, and of Antoine, who had spent the same spring deciding between a state school his parents could cover and a private one that would have meant loans like these. Antoine had chosen the state school and made acerbic jokes about it all year, but Evan had watched him at the deposit table in April, signing with a strange, quiet satisfaction. At the time it had looked like defeat. Now it looked like something closer to sense, though he wasn't sure the two things couldn't be the same thing wearing different clothes.

"Can I open something?" he said. "An account. Here."

Luc raised an eyebrow. "You have money?"

"I have the graduation checks. Six hundred. They're in an envelope in my glovebox because I keep meaning to deposit them." It was true; the envelope had ridden around with him for three weeks, a small act of delay he hadn't examined.

Luc pulled up a form, and Evan filled it out at the little shelf with the chained pens, printing his information in the careful way of someone who has watched a family member's numbers go wrong. Six hundred dollars, he understood, would not become a fortune. The chart's bend took decades, took patience he wasn't sure he had. But the same substrate that had eaten his sister's balance, interest laid on interest, would be working for him instead, and that symmetry struck him as almost elegant until he remembered that elegance had nothing to do with fairness, that the mathematics was indifferent to which of them it helped.

His sister came back from Mr. Nolan's counter with a folder and a plan and eyes that were dry but rimmed red. She looked at the deposit slip in Evan's hand.

"Look at you," she said. "A saver."

"Somebody in this car should be."

She almost smiled. Outside, the afternoon had gone gold on the parking lot, and she unlocked the car doors with a bleat of the horn. Evan slid the deposit receipt into his pocket, the paper still warm from the printer, and ran his thumb along its edge before he got in.

activity: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
knowledge_domain: how a poll's margin of error and sample size limit what its numbers can say
fact: A poll's stated margin of error applies to each candidate's share; the margin of error for the lead between two candidates is about twice as large.
story:
Karim sent the message at eleven at night, which was how Karim sent everything, as though urgency could incapacitate the rest of the world's ability to sleep. "look at this," he wrote, followed by a link, followed by three fire emojis, followed by "ruzek 48 salas 44. margin of error 3. it's over. she won."

Leo sat at his desk with the poll open in one tab and a college essay draft, two hundred words of pure mush, open in another. The draft was due Friday. The poll was due, apparently, now.

"why are you awake," Leo typed.

"why are YOU awake"

Fair. Leo clicked the link anyway. The numbers were there just as Karim said: Ruzek 48, Salas 44, margin of error plus or minus 3 points, sample of 1,100 likely voters. Beneath the numbers there was a headline calling it a "commanding lead," which struck Leo as a lot of confidence from people who had also printed, further down the page, the words "plus or minus."

"you want to bet or not," Karim wrote. "twenty bucks. easy money. she's up 4 and the margin is 3. even if it's off by the whole 3 she still wins."

Leo leaned back. His chair made its usual complaint. Somewhere below the headline the poll's own website said something in small print about methodology, and he started reading it the way you read the terms of service, which is to say at first not at all, then with dawning suspicion.

"hold on," he typed. "the margin of error is for each candidate's share."

"so"

"so it's not for the difference."

There was a pause long enough that Leo switched tabs and deleted a sentence from his essay, the one about how statistics had "opened his eyes," which even he admitted was garbage. When he came back, Karim had sent a question mark, then another one.

Leo typed slowly, feeling his way. "Each number has its own wiggle. Her 48 could be 45. His 44 could be 47. So the gap between them has both wiggles in it. The margin for the lead is about twice as big."

"that's not a thing"

"it's a thing"

"prove it"

Which was, Leo had to admit, a reasonable demand, since he had just arrived at the idea himself in the last ninety seconds and was mostly sure. He opened a new tab and typed the question into a search bar, and the internet, which had lately been an alluvial plain of nonsense spreading in every direction, actually gave him something clean: a statistics site, plain text, no ads, explaining that a poll's stated margin of error applied to each candidate's share, and the margin of error for the lead between two candidates was about twice as large. He read it twice. Six points, roughly, not three. A 4-point lead inside a 6-point margin. Not commanding. Not over.

He copied the link and sent it.

Karim did not reply for a while. Leo used the time to look at the sample size line again, 1,100, and found that the small print said a bigger sample made the margin smaller, but slowly, and that the poll was one of several taken the same week, some with Salas ahead. He had walked into the article expecting a verdict and had found instead a morass of caveats, each one individually reasonable, collectively the reason nobody he knew could say anything about the election without yelling.

"ok," Karim finally wrote. "but it's still 4 points."

"it's still 4 points," Leo agreed.

"so she's probably still ahead"

"probably, yeah. but 'probably' was doing a lot of work in that sentence you sent me at eleven p.m."

"fine. no bet then"

"no bet"

There was one more silence, and then Karim wrote, "addisyn already took the bet btw. she took salas. she says everyone's mad at ruzek about the water thing and the polls lag behind." Leo read that twice. He had not thought about the water thing at all. He had thought about the numbers, and the numbers had seemed like the whole building, and now it turned out there was a building under the building.

He pulled up the essay draft, deleted the sentence about statistics opening his eyes, and sat there for a moment with his hands off the keyboard. In the tab behind the draft, the poll glowed quietly, 48 and 44, as confident as ever about nothing in particular.

"you should tell her," he typed to Karim. "before she counts the money."

"she says the water thing is worth 6 points and you can't put that in a margin"

Leo looked at the numbers one more time. Then he picked up his phone and typed, to both of them, a question he did not know the answer to: "so what do we actually know?"

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Sociologist Robert K. Merton's 1936 essay 'The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action' listed causes of unintended consequences, including ignorance, error and focusing on immediate interests over long-term ones.
story:
The badge said VOLUNTEER in faded blue letters, and Leah pinned it to her shirt collar every Thursday at four, the way she had since September. Her job was simple: refill the water pitchers on the third floor, wheel the book cart from room to room, and leave people alone if they wanted to be left alone. She was good at the last part. Most sixteen-year-olds were not, which was why Ms. Kim, the volunteer coordinator, had told her during the interview that she had the right temperament for the work, and Leah had spent a week trying to decide whether that was a compliment.

That Thursday, Sylvie was already at the cart when Leah came in, arranging paperbacks by spine color instead of author. "Luc texted me twice during bio," Sylvie said. "Council meeting ran long. Something about the cafeteria plan."

"What cafeteria plan?"

"The waste thing. You know." Sylvie rolled her eyes. "The one they've been bragging about since October."

Leah did know, vaguely. Luc had campaigned on it: the student council would cut cafeteria waste by removing the packaged salads and switching to a single hot lunch, with smaller portions, refills on request. The plan had passed. For two weeks the kitchen bins had looked almost empty, and Luc had photographed them for the morning announcements.

She took the pitchers and started down the hall. In room 312 a man watched baseball with the sound off; in 314 a woman asked for "anything with a plot, dear, not one of those books where nothing happens." Leah set a mystery in her hands and moved on. It was in 317 that she stopped, because a girl her own age sat by the window with her chemistry textbook open, a sullen look on her face that Leah recognized from her own mirror.

"Hard unit," Leah said, nodding at the page.

"Equilibrium." The girl turned the book around. "You change one thing and everything else shifts to compensate. It's annoying."

Leah refilled her water and thought about that the whole way back to the cart. She was still thinking about it when Luc appeared in the volunteer lounge at five thirty, still wearing his council lanyard, slumped into a chair across from Ms. Kim, who had come in to sign the timesheets.

"It backfired," Luc said. "The plan. Total disaster."

"How?" Sylvie asked.

"The hot lunch takes twelve minutes a plate. The line went out the door, so kids started leaving campus for lunch, and now the corner store sells out of chips by noon and the cafeteria's throwing away more food than before, because the kitchen cooks for the whole school." He pressed his palms against his eyes. "And Ms. Kim's making us write an analysis. She asked why none of us saw it coming. Like it was obvious."

"Was it?" Leah asked.

"That's the thing. It wasn't." He sat up. "Some of us said the line would be longer. But we wanted the bins to look empty for the photo, so we voted fast."

Leah carried her timesheet to the desk, but she didn't sign it. Something the girl in 317 had said was catching on a hinge in her mind, and next to it, something her father had left on the kitchen table last month: a photocopied essay, thick and old-fashioned in its phrasing, that he'd been reading for a night class. She had read the first page out of boredom. She remembered the title now with the peculiar clarity of a thing you never meant to memorize: "The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action." Robert K. Merton, 1936. She had looked him up afterward and found that the essay listed causes of unintended consequences, and that the list included ignorance, error, and the habit of focusing on immediate interests over long-term ones.

"Leah?" Sylvie was waving a hand in front of her face. "You went somewhere."

"Sorry. My dad left this essay on the counter. Sociologist. Nineteen thirty-six." She turned to Luc. "He lists reasons plans go wrong. Ignorance, error, and caring about the near future more than the far one."

Luc stared at her. "That's it. That's the whole thing. We didn't know the kitchen couldn't move faster, that's the ignorance. And some of us did the math wrong on portions, that's error. And the photo." He laughed, short and unhappy. "The photo is the third one."

Ms. Kim finished signing her own sheet and squared the papers against the desk. "I didn't assign that essay," she said. "But I'll take it."

Leah went back for the last round of pitchers while the hallway lights dimmed to their evening setting. She was honest enough with herself to admit the essay didn't fix anything; it named the hole but did not fill it, and she could not prove the council would vote differently next time, only that they would know what to call it when they didn't. Knowledge like that was not the same as control, and she was still working out how to metabolize the difference. In 312 the man had fallen asleep with the game still running, and she turned the television down without waking him, one bar at a time, until the room was quiet.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: Jeremy Bentham's 1791 panopticon was a prison design with a central tower from which inmates could be watched at any time without knowing whether they were.
story:
The message came through at 11:47 on a Tuesday: "did anyone else get flagged." Ryder had sent a screenshot of an email from the school, automated sender, no human name at the bottom. Three tardy violations recorded by the new camera system, though Ryder swore he'd been on time every day that week. The group chat, usually just memes and complaints about Mr. Oliveira's pop quizzes, went quiet for a full minute before Merrick typed, "i got one too."

Brayden sat on his bed with the phone held above his face, reading the thread twice. He hadn't gotten an email, which bothered him more than the emails themselves. The cameras had gone up over the winter break, matte white domes bolted into the hallway ceilings, and an assistant principal had come to their homeroom in January to explain that the system used software to detect "loitering patterns" and "movement anomalies." Nobody had asked what those meant. Brayden had been half asleep and had a chemistry test on his mind, and now it was March and the software was handing out detentions.

"it's racist," Merrick wrote. "it's just racist. look who got flagged, me and ryder, and look who didn't." Brayden scrolled through the class roster in his head. Merrick and Ryder were two of maybe fifteen Black kids in a school of eleven hundred. It was a sample of two. He knew that, statistically, it meant nothing, and he also knew that the same thought had crossed all three of their minds at the same second, which meant it meant something anyway.

He typed, then deleted it, then typed again. "do we actually know what it's flagging on?" Merrick's reply was instant: "wow. way to be an apologist for the robot." Brayden put the phone down on his chest and stared at the ceiling, where a water stain had spread since August into a shape like an island.

The next morning he went to Mr. Oliveira's room before first period. He hadn't planned to; his feet just took him there, past the white dome above the water fountain, its lens a small dark bead. Mr. Oliveira taught civics and kept a shelf of battered paperbacks nobody was allowed to borrow but everybody did. Brayden asked, feeling stupid, whether the school had to tell you when you were being watched.

Mr. Oliveira didn't lecture. He pulled a book off the shelf, thumbed to a marked page, and slid it across the desk. "Read that part. Tell me what you think tomorrow." Brayden read it standing up, one hand on the cold desk edge. It described a prison designed in 1791 by Jeremy Bentham, a ring of cells around a central tower, from which the inmates could be watched at any time without knowing whether they were. The word printed there was panopticon. Brayden read it twice and felt something shift, like realizing a song he'd known for years was in a different key than he'd assumed.

At work that Saturday, bagging groceries, he noticed the camera above register four for the first time in eight months of shifts. He'd never once thought about it; now he found himself keeping his back straight, keeping his phone in his pocket, laughing at a customer's joke with a kind of performed good humor. It might not even be on. That was the part that got under his skin. It didn't have to be on. He behaved as if it were, and he couldn't tell whether that was him or the camera doing the behaving.

He texted the chat from the break room: "so bentham designed this prison in 1791 called the panopticon. tower in the middle, cells all around, guards could watch you any time and you never knew if they actually were." Then, before he could second-guess: "we're the prison. the domes are the tower." Ryder replied with three skull emojis. Merrick wrote nothing for a long time, long enough that Brayden watched the "typing" bubble appear and vanish four times. Then: "ok but if it's watching everybody why does it only flag us."

Brayden walked back out to the registers with that question lodged in him like a seed. The camera might be blind. The software behind it might be neutral in intent and crooked in effect, trained on faces and patterns that looked nothing like Merrick's, and he had no way to know, no way to see inside the dome or inside the code. He rang up a woman's groceries, said have a good day, and watched himself say it, and beneath the drone of the register he was already drafting what he'd say to Mr. Oliveira on Monday, that he believed both things at once, that the watching changed everyone and that it landed hardest on some, and that he still couldn't prove either one. On his break he opened the chat again and typed, "meeting at the library sunday. we're filing a records request."

story:
The notification woke Alexis at 1:14 in the morning, and by 1:20 there were forty-one messages in the thread, a run of them in caps, one of them just a chain of exclamation points that Ludovik had clearly abandoned midway and sent anyway. Alexis sat up in bed with the phone held above his face, brightness turned all the way down, and read upward from where the argument had broken open.

Ludovik: everyone knows it was muhammed. coach found out about saturday. muhammed knew about saturday. case closed.

Then Muhammed's reply, four minutes later, typed in the flat lowercase he used when he was genuinely angry rather than performing it: that's not a case. that's not even an argument. if i told him, he'd know. he knows. you're saying because he knows, i told him.

Alexis read that twice. Something about the shape of it snagged on him, the way a zipper catches on fabric, and he got out of bed and padded to the kitchen for water so he could think standing up. The apartment was dark except for the stove clock. In the living room his younger sister had left her logic homework open on the table, and he stopped beside it without meaning to. Her worksheet had a dinner-table example printed on it, a dialogue where a kid says, if it rained the lawn is wet, the lawn is wet, so it rained, and the mother points out the window at the sprinkler. At the bottom, in the margin, someone had written the name for it in pencil: affirming the consequent.

He carried his water back to his room, phone buzzing the whole way. Ludovik was on a roll now. The accusation had a history behind it, one Alexis only half knew: something had gone wrong at the meet on Saturday, something involving Mr. Francis and a flask and a disqualification, and someone had told, and Ludovik had spent two weeks deciding it was Muhammed. The evidence was all circumstantial and all pointed the same direction, which was the direction Ludovik already wanted to look. Alexis understood the wanting. It was easier to be furious at a person than at a situation, easier to valorize loyalty by finding a traitor than to sit with the fact that loyalty had failed in ways nobody could name.

Alexis: wait. ludovik. your logic is broken and i can prove it.

He typed the sister's example, almost word for word. If it rained, the lawn is wet. The lawn is wet. So it rained. Except the sprinkler was on.

Ludovik: what does a lawn have to do with muhammed

Alexis: same shape. if muhammed told him, the coach knows. the coach knows. so muhammed told him. but other things make the coach know. like living in california doesn't mean you live in san diego. san diego is inside california, but the whole state is bigger than the one city. muhammed telling him fits inside "coach knows" but so does other stuff.

There was a long pause, the three dots appearing and disappearing, and Alexis felt the strange suspense of watching someone think in real time, the chat's pelagic silence, wide and dark, with one small light blinking at the center of it. When Ludovik finally answered, it was with a screenshot, and Alexis's stomach dropped before he had even finished loading it.

The screenshot was of their own group chat. Dated Saturday, 9:52 p.m. It showed Ludovik, in this very thread, typing the words "francis is going to lose his MIND when he finds out what we brought," followed by the name of the boy whose mother was Mr. Francis's neighbor and who had, presumably, glanced at her son's phone. Ludovik had leaked it himself. He had written the confession into the record weeks ago and spent two weeks hunting a traitor rather than scrolling back through his own messages, because the hunt felt better than the finding.

Muhammed: so it was you. the whole time it was you.

Ludovik didn't type anything for a long time. Then a single message came through, and it wasn't an apology. It was a question mark, sent to Alexis, as if the fallacy were somehow at fault, as if pointing out the broken lock made Alexis the burglar.

Alexis sat on the edge of his bed with the phone warm in his hand. He believed now that Muhammed hadn't told, but he noticed he couldn't prove it the way he could prove the lawn example, couldn't run it backward and get certainty out. The sprinkler had merely become another thing that was possible. He started typing, deleted it, started again.

Alexis: i'm not saying he's innocent. i'm saying you don't know. neither do i. that's the whole point.

Muhammed's reply was a thumbs up, which felt like an encapsulation of three years of friendship compressed into one small gray gesture. Ludovik left the chat at 2:03. The thread sat there, 184 messages, the last one visible on Alexis's screen, and beneath it his own cursor blinking in the empty box.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In Classical-era sonata-form movements, the exposition is often marked with repeat signs, so the performer plays it twice before the development begins.
story:
Jordyn arrived at Iris's house with a photocopied score of Mozart's Sonata in A major rolled up under her arm like a baton, and a theory worksheet folded into her back pocket, soft from being handled on the bus. The worksheet wanted the exposition, the development, and the recapitulation marked with brackets and measure numbers, and it was due Monday, and she had stared at it for two nights without knowing where the brackets began. Iris's kitchen smelled of cardamom because her mother was simmering something on the back burner, and Walid was already at the table with his laptop open, headphones half off one ear.

"Listen to this first," he said, before Jordyn had even sat down. "The whole thing, no score, just ears." He pressed play.

The opening was neat and bright, the kind of melody that sounded like it was introducing itself at a party. Jordyn closed her eyes and tried to follow it. First theme, she thought, then a bridge that moved somewhere else, then a second theme with more ornament on it, softer, in a different key. Then the opening came back. Exactly the same, measure for measure, or so close she couldn't tell.

She opened her eyes. Walid was frowning at his laptop. "Is the recording broken? He literally started over."

"That's what I said," Iris said, pulling mugs down from the shelf. "First time I listened to it I thought the file was corrupted. My dad had to check."

Jordyn unrolled the score across the table, weighting the curling corners with Iris's mugs and a bowl of pistachios. She had compartmentalized her listening up to now: school music was analysis, and the music she loved on her own was feeling, and the two lived in separate rooms she never opened at the same time. But the repeat was standing in the doorway between them. She ran her finger along the staves until, at the double bar after the second theme, she found two dots stacked like a colon, and then, back at the very beginning, the same two dots facing the other way. She knew those signs. She had played them in recital pieces since she was nine without ever once asking what they were doing there, which felt, suddenly, like a congenital blindness she was only now noticing she had.

"Wait," she said. "It's not a mistake. There are repeat signs." She tapped the score. "In these sonata movements, the exposition gets marked with repeat signs, so the pianist plays it twice before the development begins." Walid leaned over, and she traced the path for him: play to the double bar, jump back to the start, do it all again, then continue.

"So the recording is fine and Mozart wanted it?" Walid scrubbed backward in the file anyway, listening for a hidden flaw. "Twice the same thing on purpose."

"It's not the same thing, though." Jordyn said it before she had thought it through, and then found she meant it. "The second time you hear the opening, you already know where it's going. You know there's a second theme coming, in a different key, so the first theme sounds different. Like rereading the first chapter of a book after you've finished it." She was thinking of the ontology of it, though she didn't say that word aloud, didn't quite dare: what is a theme, actually, when the notes are identical but the meaning isn't? Was the thing itself the sound, or the sound plus everything you'd learned since the last time?

Iris sat down and pulled the score toward herself. "Then where's the development? After the repeat ends?"

They listened again, all three of them crowded close to the laptop speaker, and Jordyn marked with a pencil where the music stopped being tidy. The material from both themes started breaking apart, wandering through keys that never settled, sequences climbing and slipping. Her bracket wobbled because her hand wobbled. "Here," she said. "It stops introducing itself and starts arguing."

The recapitulation was easier to find, and also stranger. The first theme returned in the home key, but not perfectly; the bridge had been rewritten, trimmed of its modulating push, and when the second theme arrived it stayed in A major instead of traveling. Jordyn wrote her last bracket and then sat back. "So the recap is the exposition again," she said slowly, "but changed. The second theme comes home." She wondered whether that was the point of the whole form, or whether she was inventing a point the way people invent constellations, connecting dots that had nothing to do with each other. She couldn't decide, and the worksheet had no box for that.

Walid filled in his grid with the measure numbers she called out, and Iris copied the brackets in colored pen, which looked so much better than Jordyn's penciled wobble that Jordyn asked to take a photo. In the photo, the repeat signs showed as two small pairs of dots, like punctuation the piece was breathing around.

"One more time through?" Iris asked, her hand already reaching for the track. "I want to hear the second exposition the way you said. Like rereading the first chapter."

Jordyn said, "Same chapter, different reader," and pressed play.

story:
The food bank shared the library's basement, which meant Colton's first shift began with the smell of old carpet and canned tomatoes, and with a hand-drawn sign taped to a book cart that said VOLUNTEERS THIS WAY, the arrow pointing at the men's washroom.

"That arrow's a lie," said a boy behind him, holding a clipboard. "I'm Yann. I've been here four weeks, and the arrow has always been a lie." He was, Colton learned within a minute, trying to earn a scholarship by logging community hours, and had brought his own clipboard because the food bank's clipboards kept going missing. "Somebody's taking them. That's my theory. A clipboard black market."

Down a hallway that the arrow had failed to mention, folding tables had been set up between the microfiche cabinets, and a woman named Ms. Malik was assigning stations. She gave Yann the intake desk, where he could hover over his clipboard like a dragon over gold. She gave a tall boy called Maximilien the sorting table, and he groaned theatrically, because Maximilien, it turned out, had opinions about the dignity of squash. "Nobody has ever wanted a can of squash," he announced to the room. "It arrives here, and it leaves here, and nobody in between has loved it."

Colton got the registration table, which meant greeting people as they came in. His mother had signed him up, partly for the hours and partly, he suspected, because she thought it would be good for him in some way she couldn't name, and he'd resisted, and then stopped resisting, and now here he was, not entirely sure which of those had been the real decision.

The first hour was slower than he'd imagined. An older man came through and took bread and peanut butter and, after a long negotiation with Maximilien, one can of squash. A woman with two kids let the younger one pick the pasta shape, which took a while because the options were elbows or nothing. Between arrivals, the three boys argued in low voices about whether the library's copier, humming behind them, sounded like a torpid frog or a torpid bee, an argument Maximilien insisted could be settled.

Then Ms. Malik brought down a box of pamphlets for the table, historical ones, from an anniversary a few years back, and Colton flipped through one while he waited. "Wait," he said. "This says Canada's first food bank opened in Edmonton on January 16, 1981."

"1981?" Yann abandoned his clipboard long enough to come look. "That's, like, my dad was already alive. I thought food banks were just, I don't know, old. Victorian. Gruel-based."

"Edmonton," Maximilien said, as though the city itself were suspect. "In January. That's the most Canadian thing I've ever heard. 'It's minus forty and the economy is broken, let's invent a food bank.'"

Colton kept turning the pamphlet over. He had been picturing the food bank as something permanent, a piece of the country's skeleton, and it bothered him a little, in a way he couldn't quite close his hand around, that it was younger than his uncle. It hadn't been waiting here all along. Somebody had decided, on a specific day, that it needed to exist, and then it did, and now he was sitting at a table in its basement arguing about squash.

"It's like finding out bridges were invented in 1981," he said.

"Bridges are older than that," Yann said. "I want to be clear that I know bridges are older than that."

A woman came in then with a stroller, so the conversation broke off, and Colton found that the practice of the table came back to him easily: the sign-in sheet, the gentle steering toward the bread that would go stale tomorrow. He was bad at the small jokes adults made, the weather, the "keeping you busy," and he could feel himself performing cheerfulness for a few seconds before it settled into something more honest, which was just paying attention to her, to which shelf she looked at longest.

When the rush thinned, Yann drifted back over, and there was a subtlety to his tone that Colton was starting to recognize as pre-clipboard-speech. "Some of these people come every week," Yann said. "Same people. Every week. I've started writing down, like, what they take, so we can put it out where they can find it."

"You're profiling soup preferences."

"I'm improving the system."

Colton looked down the room at Maximilien, who had arranged the squash cans into a small, doomed pyramid, and at Ms. Malik, who was letting him do it, and he thought that probably the right position was somewhere between Yann's clipboard and Maximilien's pyramid: that the thing mattered, and it was also, mostly, cans. Whether the first people in Edmonton in 1981 had felt that same confusion, he genuinely didn't know, and the pamphlet didn't say.

"Okay," he said, standing up. "But before you improve anything, come look at this. Maximilien built something and it's about to fall."

They turned together, just in time to watch the top can of squash roll off the pyramid and land, with a hollow, perfect clank, on the concrete floor.

"Not my can," Maximilien said. "I never touched that can."
